subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS

speechtext: Hon. MAURICE DUPRE (Acting Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 84, to amend the Judges Act.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
The provisions
of this bill appear to violate contracts between the crown and members of the judiciary. Perhaps my hon. friend would explain to us on the second reading whether that is the case or not, and if it is the case, on what grounds he justifies the measure at all.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
This bill does not interfere
directly or indirectly with the tenure of office or the salary of judges. It has to do entirely with the capacity of judges to earn their salary after they have been appointed. It has long been recognized by parliament that tenure of office during good behaviour can only be enjoyed by judges who have the capacity to perform their duty. _ Already we have in the Judges Act a provision whereby a judge who by reason of age or infirmity becomes incapacitated or disabled from the due execution of his office shall cease to be paid or to receive or be entitled to receive any further salary. That is in section 28 of the Judges Act, chapter 105 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927.
The present amendment does not deal with total incapacity, and it expressly provides that it shall not modify or affect the operation of the provision which I have just mentioned. What is dealt with in the bill before us is partial incapacity. I think the only real question of policy arising for discussion is the old one of what may reasonably be done in the public interest to prevent a judge whose

capacity is undoubtedly diminished by advancing age from continuing to hold office and to draw the same emoluments as are being drawn by his younger brethren who are carrying the burden of the work. As hon. gentlemen know, parliament has already acted upon the principle that the judges whose tenure of office is within the jurisdiction of the dominion shall cease to hold office when they attain the age of seventy-five. This provision with regard to county judges will be found in section 26 of the Judges Act. With regard to the judges of the supreme court and of the exchequer court there was a long debate in this house in 1927 in which my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) participated, and this same provision I mentioned as applying to the judges of the supreme court and the exchequer court will be found in subsection 2 of section 24 of the Judges Act, and in sections 30 and 38 of the Judges Act, which is chapter 105 of the statutes of 1927.
In the year 1927 there were three measures proposed dealing with the judiciary by my hon. friend from Quebec East, as Minister of Justice, namely, a bill to amend the Supreme Court Act, a bill to amend the Exchequer Court Act, and a bill to amend the Judges Act, so as to provide for the retirement of judges at the age of seventy-five. At that time the opinion was expressed that the good administration of justice depends not only upon the integrity and right sense of justice of the high officials who sit on the bench, but also on their capacity to carry on their duties. It has been said that when a man has attained the age of seventy-five he may not have the mental and physical endurance that is demanded in the exercise of his duties. It is a debatable question whether seventy-five years, or eighty or seventy-eight is the right age, but the general consensus of opinion seems to be that seventy-five years might be the limit.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I shall be glad to answer my hon. friend when we are in committee.
In 1927 my hon. friend from Quebec East, as Minister of Justice, presented the amendments to which I referred a moment ago, and in introducing his bill to amend the Judges Act said:
This resolution precedes the introduction of three bills; one to amend the Supreme Court Act, another to amend the Exchequer Court Apt and the third to amend the Judges Act. The first clause of the resolution provides for the granting of a salary for one additional judge of the Supreme Court of Canada. The two other clauses of the resolution, which have been prepared by the officers of the house from copies of the bills which have been supplied to them, provide for the retirement of the judges of the Supreme court or of the Exchequer Court of Canada when they have reached the age of seventy-five years. These are the financial arrangements to supply them with a pension to which they would otherwise be entitled.
Mr. Boys: Is that voluntary retirement?
Mr. Lapointe:	No, they would cease to
hold office at the age of seventy-five years. These two changes are made for the same reasons. The Supreme Court of Canada is the highest tribunal of the land and it is of the utmost importance that it should have and retain the confidence of the people and be maintained in the highest state of efficiency.
These words are to be found in Hansard of March 10, 1927, at page 1079. Then, on the following page the ex-Minister of Justice added:
There is another consideration which applies to the provision making retirement compulsory at seventy-five years of age. Members of the bar come to argue eases before the Supreme court from distant parts of the country, and the court must be complete and well organized in order to hear these cases when counsel come to Ottawa for that purpose. Such cases cannot be adjourned except at considerable expense and to the disadvantage of the litigants and the members of the bar as well. These considerations apply as well to the other clauses of the bill making the retirement of the judges of the Supreme court and the Exchequer court compulsory at the age of seventy-five years.
We subscribe to that principle. The present bill does not affect the federal court but only those judges sitting in the superior courts of any provinoe or of the Yukon territory. The
argument I may present to the house was presented by the ex-Minister of Justice when at page 1081 of the same volume he said:
I was reading in the library that in the country to the south they have the same conditions with regard to their federal courts. The constitution of the United States enacts that the judges of these courts shall be appointed and remain in office during good behaviour, and the government has never been able, although it has tried, in many instances, to make their retirement compulsory. The United States has endeavoured to deal with the situation by giving a pension equal to their full salary to judges who, having been in office at least ten years and reaching the age of seventy, desire to be superannuated. That was an invitation to them to retire, because they would have a pension equal to their salary; but experience shows that most of them preferred to remain on the bench, even though they were given the right to a full pension when they reached the age of seventy. Fortunately we have not the same obstacle to meet as far as our federal courts are concerned, and I have come to the conclusion, having not only consulted with but received suggestions from the members of the bar and I might even say from members of the judiciary themselves, that this is a good provision to enact. That is why I am introducing these bills.
Then, answering the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) on March 25, 1927, the ex-Minister of Justice is reported ait page 1562 of Hansard as follows:
I am sorry the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George does not agree with me on the age limit; I will admit that there is ground for a difference of opinion in that matter. I can assure my hon. friend that only after serious consideration and after having discussed this matter with many people who have a deep interest in strengthening the Supreme Court of Canada, did I take it upon my responsibility as Minister of Justice to introduce this Bill. I quite agree with my hon. friend that there are eminent judges who are wholly qualified to act as such after they have reached the age of seventy-five years, but as the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) has said, they are rather the exception. May I quote to the house the words of a man who has been Secretary of State in the United States. Mr. Chief Justice Taft, concerning this very question. In a book entitled Popular Government at page 158 he writes:
And this is our argument, too:
" Congress has passed a law providing that all federal judges may retire after a service of ten years, upon attaining the age of seventy. The law is in form not compulsory because I presume it was thought doubtful whether Congress had any power to retire judges, even though they continue the full salary as a life pension."
The constitution of the United States makes the tenure of office of a judge there during good behaviour, and congress has no right to make it compulsory.
Mr. Cahan:	That applies to federal judges
only.
Mr. Lapointe: To federal judges only. Chief Justice Taft goes on to say:
Judges Act-Mr. Dupre

" I think the absence of power in Congress to do this is a defect. There is no doubt that there are judges at seventy who have ripe judgments, active minds, and much physical vigour, and that they are able to perform their judicial duties in a very satisfactory way. Yet in a majority of cases -when men come to be seventy, they have lost vigour, their minds are not as active, their senses are not as acute, and their willingness to undertake great labour is not so great as in younger men, and as we ought to have in judges who are to perform the enormous task which falls to the lot of Supreme court justices. In the public interest, therefore, it is better that we lose the services of the exceptions who are good judges after they are seventy and avoid the presence on the bench of men who are not able to keep up with the work, or to perform it satisfactorily. The duty of a Supreme court judge is more than merely taking in the point at issue between the parties, and deciding it. It frequently involves a heavy task in reading records and writing opinions. It thus is a substantial drain upon one's energy. When most men reach seventy, they are loath thoroughly to investigate cases where such work involves real physical indurance.
That is not all. In 1922 a bill concerning the province of Saskatchewan was presented in the Senate. At that time Senator Bennett speaking on the bill quoted the words of the Hon. Mr. Perron. They are found at page 184 of the Debates of the Senate for that year and are as follows:
In this matter, he said he was in absolute harmony with Premier Tasehereau in idea and ideal, and if it %vas that justice was delayed through the inability-owing to ill health-of certain judges, and if they did not realize their responsibilities and resign, then "it would be the painful duty of the bar to seek legislation that would meet the contingency".
Speaking on that bill the Hon. Mr. Dan-durand, then leader of the Senate and a member of the government, added the following words:
The great problem is to find within the terms of the constitution a way to bring to the attention of the judges the necessity for their retiring without recourse being had to the very solemn process of an address by both branches of this parliament.
These words are to be found at page 189 of the Debates of the Senate for the year 1922. Later, on the 12th of May of the same year, Hon. Senator Barnard speaking on Bill No. 19, an act to amend the Judges Act, made the following proposition, which I would call to the attention of my hon. friend the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe):
The governor in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice that any judge has by reason of his age or infirmities become unable to properly perform his duty and upon three months' notice does not retire, may order that the salary of such judge shall be reduced to $1 a year from a date to be named, and thereafter such judge shall until he retires be
[Mr. Dupr&l
paid no more than that amount, but on his so retiring he shall be entitled to the retiring allowance which would have been paid to him had he retired immediately before such order was made.
Then speaking of this amendment the leader of the Senate, a member of the then government, the Hon. Mr. Dandurand, added the following words which will be found on page 214:
I confess that my first impression was that this proposed legislation should rather be embodied in a separate bill to amend the Judges Act, because it would then be taken up with more solemnity and would attract the attention of all members of this chamber and would receive due consideration.
And he then said:
I am in sympathy with the ends sought to be attained, and will do nothing to prevent its adoption. If this chamber thinks we ought to proceed immediately with the adoption of this amendment, attaching it to the present bill, well and good. We may conclude, however, that it is better to make the amendment a separate bill.
Therefore in moving this bill we present to this house less drastic legislation than that which has already been proposed by the former government.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) has quoted extensively from remarks I made in the house in 1927 on the bill relating to federal court judges. Modesty precludes me from adding that the best part of his speech is the quotations which he made.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: And the best part of the hon. gentleman's speech in 1927 was his quotation from Chief Justice Taft.

I do not say it. But I would suggest to my hon. friend that he might have read another three or four lines from that address of mine when that resolution was introduced in 1927, on page 1080. He came very close to that sentence but he stopped there. Here is what I stated:
The sections of the British North America Act dealing with the judicature are Nos. 96 to 101. Section 99 states that the judges of the superior courts shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons. According to the enactment, the tenure of the judges of the high courts of Canada is really a life tenure

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: We all agree with that.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
and this parliament has no right to retire them compulsorily at any time during good behaviour.

Judges Act-Mr. Lapointe
The difference between that position and that of judges of the federal courts which were constituted by this parliament is quite apparent, because there was nothing in the constitution which prevented us fixing an age limit for their tenure of office. Not so with the judges who will be affected by the present bill. I have quoted in extenso section 99 of the British North America Act applying to judges who will come under the provisions of this bill.
My objection to this bill is that again, as on previous occasions, it is sought to do indirectly what cannot be done directly. The effect of this bill will be to say to the judges: We cannot retire you, under the constitution you are appointed for life, but we will starve you out of office when you are 75 years of age by reducing your salary. Mr. Speaker, I will also quote a few words from a prominent gentleman, which a thousand times more apply to the present bill than to the one which was discussed in 1927, because at that time we were doing something which we had the right to do under the constitution. Possibly my hon. friend will also say that this will be the best part of my speech. I think it will be an effective part of my objection to the present bill. When that bill to retire the judges of the supreme court and of the federal courts generally was before this house for the first time the right hon. Prime Minister, who was then the member for Calgary-I do not know whether he was leader of the opposition-made a speech in which he raised the question of the contract which came into existence between the judges and the state when they accepted their appointment to office on the judiciary. That was on March 25, 1927, at pages 1556-7. I will quote only one sentence. The right hon. the present leader of the government said at that time:
What we are now doing involves a breach of the contract between the individual who holds office at the present time and the state, because his patent of office declares that he shall hold office during life or during good behaviour. He is still alive.
And then my right hon. friend suggested that if the bill becomes law we should at least provide that the judges who were then in office, who would come under the law, should be paid their full salary during their lifetime. My hon. friend the member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) the present Secretary of State, took also a very strong stand on the bill then before the house, very strong indeed. He reiterated these objections the following year. On May 29, 1929, as reported at page 2951 of Hansard, when I as Minister of Justice moved the second reading of a bill to amend 53719-303
the Supreme Court Act, my hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) spoke as follows in the course of his remarks:
In case a judge has been appointed for life it is a serious breach of contract when that judge is compelled to retire at an age and at a time when he is thoroughly equipped physically and intellectually for the performance of his judicial duties, and especially in view of the fact that his compulsory retirement necessitates his taking a pension which is very considerably less than the salary which would otherwise be paid to him under his contract with the state.
On the same occasion my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) also spoke and he said, as reported at page 2951:
That judge undoubtedly has a contract with the state which entitles him to receive a salary for life or until such time as he resigns.
And at page 2952, the right hon. gentleman
said:
I think the government would be well advised to consider whether or not, in all cases of this kind where a contract has thus been, amended, the judge should receive full salary.
On the same page my right hon. friend added:
I think we must have regard to the terms and conditions under which the original contract was made. Although it may seem out of the ordinary that a judge should draw full salary when he is retired compulsorily, nevertheless, good faith and morals-
I call the attention of the house to those words:
-good faith and morals, in my judgment, impose upon us that obligation, and it is an obligation which we should not lightly disregard.
Later on he said:
I do not believe that the Canadian people would approve of our departing from the general principle that the government must, as in times past, have respect for the sanctity of a contract made between a servant of the crown when he entered the employment of the state.
We are hearing a good deal these days about the sanctity of contracts, but it seems to apply only to bondholders who do not pay taxes to the country. But in the very words of the present Prime Minister, there was a contract, and the words which are used to-day with regard to those who loaned their money to the state were used at that time-sanctity of contract.

speechtext:
I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but may I ask him how he reconciles his view with the one expressed by the Hon. Mr. Dandurand, a former leader of the Senate, when he said that a judge after seventy-five years might receive a salary of only $1 a year.

Judges Act-Mr. Lapointe

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I would suggest that the hon. gentleman address his question to the Hon. Mr. Dandurand. Really, I do not see why he should interrupt my speech to ask that question. Now, sir, this principle, which was so strongly adhered to by members of the present government a few years ago they still adhered to last year. Take the debates of last session on the bill to reduce the salaries of civil servants, and there you will find the words of the Prime Minister giving as a justification for not having included the judges in that legislation the fact that there was a difference and that there was involved the question of contract as between them and the state. And in order to reach them the government had to take another course, whereby they increased the income tax of the judges so that they should be compelled to pay that ten per cent, because the constitution, and the principles which seemed to have been accepted by the Prime Minister and by everyone, precluded any other course than that being taken.
In the strong battle waged by my hon. friend the Secretary of State and by the Prime Minister, and after I had received communications, verbal and otherwise, from various members of the bar in Canada, I made up my mind that we should accede to the request that was made, and an amendment was adopted by this house covering the case of those judges who had been appointed before the new law was enacted, so that they should receive their full salary after retirement. This has applied to Mr. Justice Mignault. At the time this bill became law the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White) asked whether it would apply to Mr. Justice Mignault and on my replying yes, he said he approved heartily but he regretted that it had taken so long to perform this elementary act of justice. Other judges who have been retired under this law are also receiving their full salary; I might cite the instance of Mr. Justice Audette, who is drawing his full salary.
This bill affects judges who, under the constitution, mind you, not under the law but under the British North America Act, are appointed for life, and we do not even provide for payment to them of their full salary as this parliament has done for the judges of federal courts who came under the law which my hon. friend has quoted as his authority for the present bill.
Now, as to the advisability of judges being retired when they have reached the age of seventy-five, I quite admit that personally I believe there are pros and cons on the pro-

position, and I would rather think that there are more advantages than disadvantages. If this could be done in a direct, honest, straightforward way, I would not be prepared to say that I would vote against the second reading of this bill; but I am opposed to this roundabout, indirect way of doing what parliament cannot do directly. My hon. friend said: Well, we want to pay judges who are over seventy-five years of age reduced salaries because of their reduced capacity for earning. Let me remind him, and he knows well that in our own city, our own district, it was possibly the oldest judge who, for many years after he had reached the age of seventy-five, was, until quite recently, when he was stricken by illness, most active and doing the greatest amount of business on the bench.

I am going to read that section to this house so that there may be no misapprehension as to what is the existing law with respect to these cases:
28. Any judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or of the Exchequer Court of Canada, or of any superior court in Canada, or any local judge in admiralty of the Exchequer Court of Canada or any judge of a county court, who is found by the governor in council, upon report of the Minister of Justice, to have become, by reason of age or infirmity, incapacitated or disabled from the due execution of his office, shall, notwithstanding anything in this act contained, cease to be paid or to receive or to be entitled to receive any further salary, if the facts respecting the incapacity or disability are first made the subject of inquiry and report in the manner hereinafter provided, and the judge is given reasonable notice of the time and place appointed for the inquiry and is afforded an opportunity by himself or his counsel of being heard thereat and of cross-examination of witnesses and of adducing evidence on his own behalf.
2.	The governor in council may, for the purpose of making inquiry into the facts respecting the incapacity or disability of any such judge, issue a commission of inquiry to one or more judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, or of the Exchequer Court of Canada, or to one or more judges of any superior court in Canada, empowering him or them to make such inquiry and report, and may by such commission confer upon the person or persons appointed full power to summon before mm [DOT]or them any person or witness and to require him to give evidence on oath orally or in writing, or on solemn affirmation, if entitled to affirm in civil matters, and to produce such documents and things as the commissioner or commissioners deem requisite to the full investigation of the matters into which he or they are appointed to inquire: and the commissioner or commissioners shall have the same power to enforce the attendance of such person or witness and to compel him to give evidence as is vested in any superior court of the province in which the inquiry is being conducted.
3.	Nevertheless His Majesty shall by letters patent under the Great Seal of Canada grant unto any judge who has been so found by the governor in council to be incapacitated or disabled by reason of age or infirmity as aforesaid. and who resigns his office, the annuity which he might have received if he had resigned at the time when he ceased to be entitled to receive any further salary.

Then paragraph 4:
4. Nothing in this act contained shall prevent the governor in council from granting to any judge so found to be incapacitated or disabled as aforesaid leave of absence for such

period as the governor in council, in view of all the circumstances of the case, may consider just or appropriate, and if leave of absence be granted the salary of the judge shall continue to be paid during the period of leave of absence so granted.
That was passed in 1922 and, as I say, is the revision of section 2 of chapter 29 of the statutes of that year. Has the true significance of that statute become apparent to this house? It provided a method, now charged to be indirect, of dealing with a situation that had caused much criticism throughout the Dominion of Canada, which was referred to by Senator Dandurand in the Senate and which has been referred to in many parts of this country as constituting little short of what one eminent man described as a public scandal. Observe the language. No one charged the hon. gentleman then with endeavouring to do indirectly what he could not do directly; no one then charged that political reasons were responsible for this action, which gave the governor in council the power to terminate the contract, to say that he should receive no salary at all-not that he should receive two-thirds of his salary but that he should be deprived of all salary-unless he resigned. That is the law we find to-day upon the statute books. We did not make it, but confronted with a situation which in my judgment had to be dealt with, the only manner in which it could be dealt with was what? First, we could issue a commission to inquire as to the fitness, by reason of age, of men whom this high court of parliament had declared should not discharge their functions longer if they were seventy-five years of age, a limitation which we said made it impossible for a county court judge to continue in office, and which compelled a justice of the highest court in Canada to retire. Now' because we endeavour, by the use of decent methods, to accomplish directly what this statute was endeavouring to accomplish indirectly, it is charged that we are being actuated by political motives.
Does the house understand and appreciate the difficulty with regard to complaints that are made with respect to men who continue to hold judicial office but who are only capable of giving concentrated attention to an argument for two hours a day or less? Does the house understand what is involved by continuing those men in office, while litigants complain vigorously because there is no method by which the situation can be met? If they decline to accede to polite requests what is left to this parliament to do? Are we to be charged with political considerations

Judges Act-Mr. Bennett
with respect to a matter of this kind when a statute such as this was placed upon the statute books of this country by the government of which the hon. gentleman was a member? That is most unfair. There is the statute; it provides for a commission of inquiry to determine the fitness of the judge. Listen to these words; the commission is to determine his fitness to discharge his duties, by reason of disability, age or infirmity. Those are the words incorporated in the statute by my hon. friend.

That is just what I am

subsequently enact? That seventy-five was the testing age. No longer a case for inquiry. Seventy-five was definitely and positively the age, and when that age was reached the office was vacant. That is not our act. We are not responsible for that. I said when that act was before the house that I had grave doubts about whether the age should be seventy-five or eighty, but after listening to what was said and reading the authorities, including Mr. Justice Taft's view, I concluded that seventy-five was a reasonable age to fix.
Now, confronted with that situation, and without going into detail, trying in every sense to avoid the discussion of personalities in this parliament with respect to the men or the age of the men who hold office, trying to eliminate all that, I put it to the house, in view of that legislation and the difficulties that the then Minister of Justice had, and the reasons that influenced him to declare by statute in 1927 that age, which is the word used in 1922, should mean seventy-five years, whether this government is not just and fair and equitable in every sense of the word when it says that when a judge attains the age of seventy-five he shall be paid in accordance with his reduced capacity, namely, two-thirds of his salary? There is no violation of contract there. The implied term of every contract is that as long as he is fit he is to be paid, and being unfit he is not to be paid, and that has been embodied in the terms of a statute that was passed not under this government, but under the government in 1922. Now we are applying the principle of that and are merely saying, arbitrarily if you will: When you have reached the age of seventy-five in a provincial court your salary shall be two-thirds of what it was when you were at your high point of efficiency. Hon. gentlemen will realize that there is a vast improvement in that over what the provisions of the statute provide. Section 28 of the existing Judges Act says that if the inquiry determines that by reason of age he is unfit- to give that close attention to his duties which their importance demands he shall receive nothing at all. That is the law which my hon. friend's government saw fit to enact, and there are people who say they have no reason to quarrel with that, and I am not quarrelling with it at the moment.
Now is it desirable in view of the attitude taken by this parliament in fixing seventy-five as the age at which judges of the Supreme Court of Canada are declared incapable of discharging their duties effectively and efficiently-

speechtext:
Will the

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
Section 2 is to provide
for the case-there is one case in this country at the moment-of a judge who will have attained the age of seventy-five by the first of July and will not have served fifteen years. He is protected and will get his annuity. That is what the section is for, to provide against any injustice being done by reducing to nothing the pay of a judge who has attained the age of seventy-five and has not put in the full fifteen years. But there is something more than that. The effect of this bill will be to prevent men over sixty being appointed to the bench of the superior courts, and every member of the profession knows that that is not only desirable but essential. It will ensure that men of vigour at least in the profession will be appointed to the bench. It means that unless tney are under sixty when appointed they will not have served the fifteen years to entitle them to secure the pension at seventy-five.

In Great Britain, where they have imposed an age limit with respect to county courts much less than ours, they have no age limit with respect t>o their judges, and there have been eminent men who past the age of seventy-five have discharged judicial duties, notably in the courts of appeal. One of the most eminent who retired not long ago after he had passed the age of eighty said once very frankly, "If there is any question ever raised in the House of Commons with respect to my remaining and discharging judicial duties I shall of course feel that I have outlived my usefulness and shall retire." It was mentioned in the house, and he retired.
There was criticism made in the House of Commons with respect to the judicial committee and the age of its members, and if anyone will take the judicial committee as at present constituted he will find how young in years are the men w'ho constitute 'that committee.
I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that I think it is most unfair to suggest a political motive behind this bill. I am perfectly willing to be charged with political considerations in some matters, but in a matter that affects the profession to which I myself belong I claim that I have been influenced by no consideration other than the public weal. What is more, I know what the judgment of litigants is who have to have their cases considered and adjudicated upon by men past the age of eighty years, and who in the very nature of things have not the physical stamina to concentrate their powers in such a way as to enable them to grapple with the problems that arise for consideration by courts of justice. If I had purely political reasons behind the judgment which I have formed in this matter, and which arises solely because of circumstances to which I could but will not refer, and which must be present in the mind of every one responsible for law and the maintenance of law and order in the country and the holding up to high place in the minds of the people of the judicial tribunals in Canada-I say that every man who gives any thought to it at all must realize that the same purpose is in the mind of the government that has endeavoured to do this which I believe was honestly in the mind of the government that passed section 28 in 1922. I never for a moment have thought that political considerations influenced the government in 1922 when they said that if because of age a man is unfit for his duties or is not discharging them properly he shall thereby forfeit any further pay. No one for a moment

Judges Act-Mr. Elliott
charges that; no one suggested it. It is because this parliament has decided that age means seventy-five years that further trial should be unnecessary. But if it is necessary it only drags into disrepute the very institutions which, men charged with a sense of responsibility should themselves realize first of all. They should be the first to realize conditions with respect to a matter of this kind.
I think on consideration-nay, I feel certain that on consideration the hon. member for Quebec East who gave such attention to this matter in days gone by and who made such statements in the house in 1927 when the government of which he was a member enacted the legislation to which I have referred, will acquit this government of any sense of political responsibility in dealing with this matter. For I say to him this, that if he will study the appointments which have been made to the bench since this government has assumed office he will see, at least, that no consideration-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire for a few moments to protest against this legislation. Anyone who is familiar with the bench of the province of Ontario must admit that a number of the very best, the most capable and the most active judges we have are beyond the age of seventy-five years. I believe members of the profession as well as hon. members in the house will agree with me that perhaps the keenest, the most able and the most active judge on the Ontario bench, and the one who has lost the smallest amount of time in the last ten or fifteen years, is 'the oldest judge on the bench of that province.

The difference between dealing with the matter under section 28 of the act, and dealing with it in a summary manner provided by the legislation now under consideration is that in one case the man has a chance to go before some tribunal and show whether or not he has by age, incapacity or infirmity become disabled to perform his duty.

The Prime Minister spoke about age or infirmity. I remind him that a man does not come under section 28 of the act because of age alone; it is on account of infirmity. I believe the Prime Minister knows perfectly well that a great many-

In the case of a man under 75 the factor to be considered is incapacity. Incapacity may be due to age or infirmity, but age of itself alone does not bring him within the amfait of section 28. May I point out also that in the province of Ontario, as I said before, a number of our most active, able and capable judges would be affected by this act. One member of a commission that was appointed not long ago to perform very difficult and onerous duties, involving a great deal of work and requiring great ability, was one of the judges who would be affected by this act. He was appointed not by a government of his own political complexion; he was selected on account of his ability, his physical strength and his capacity for work, as well as for the wide experience gained at the bar and on the bench.
The violation of contract feature has already been referred to; I do not intend to labour that. The fact that this is an attempt to do indirectly what cannot be done directly has also been referred to. The great objection to this proposal is that it is a breach of faith as well as a breach of contract. These men are entitled to the benefit of the act as it stood at the time of their appointment. They hold office unless they have become incapacitated, that is the present state of the law. I submit that this is the kind of legislation that should not be passed at any time, and it is particularly inappropriate at this time, as it would impose a further great burden upon the treasury of this country, by making each of those positions from which a judge is retired pay 815,000 a year, or practically so, whereas if he were not retired it would pay only 89,000. We cannot afford at the present time to increase the expenditure of the government in any way that can be avoided. So I submit that if ever it were excusable this is

not the time it should be done. If it is the wish of the government to make this provision applicable to future appointees that is quite fair. It is no breach of faith. In Ontario it operates against I think seven or eight of the most eminent judges we have ever had in the province, all of whom are now active on the bench. I cannot protest too strongly against legislation that deals so unfairly with men who have given to this country the kind of service that those men have given upon the bench.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am astonished to see such legislation presented to the house, having in view the legal ability'' and knowledge of the Prime Minister. He knows perfectly well that he is putting before this house a bill, which had he been leader of the opposition instead of Prime Minister, would have drawn thunderbolts from him. I take his own argument in the case of the bill relating to the Supreme Court of Canada; why do again in this house by special legislation what is provided against by the statute? Section 28 of chapter 105 of the revised statutes of Canada has been passed and must be applied. If a judge by his conduct or through incapacity comes under investigation under this aot he is in the same position as any other person. Let the government then investigate, and if justified impeach him if he does not resign. Our judges when appointed were, under the constitution, appointed for life. They abandoned everything when they went on the bench. The bench of Canada is composed of able and honest men. If there were exceptions I *would not care to mention them, but I do not think they exist. When they are appointed they have to cut themselves off completely from business life, leave their career behind them, give up their legal practice. If they were placed on the bench by the leader of their party it was because they were able men qualified to adorn the bench. They can no longer hqld appointments as testamentary executors, they cannot be executors of companies. They go on the 'bench and to the best of their ability administer the law of the country. They have no friends, they are completely apart in the community if they are doing their duty. The statute says that after so many years they are entitled to retire on pension; they are not obliged to go, but they may go if they want to. We cannot suppose that a person qualified to be appointed a judge would remain on the bench
if unable through sickness or other disability to discharge his duties; such an assumption would be contrary to common sense and to the opinion that all citizens have of a judge.
I think the Prime Minister will agree that the judicature is one of the four powers of the state, these powers being the sovereign, the executive, the army and the judicature. Whether legislation enacted in the past relating to judges was wise or not, if we alter it now we destroy public confidence in the bench. Judges should not be interfered with because they compose the tribunals established to administer justice. If 'this House of Commons does not abide by its contracts, how do we expect any individual in Canada to respect his contract? What this bill proposes is an expropriation of right, and if it came before a court of justice any judge would dismiss such a case. The constitution is there; you cannot act against the constitution. Of course not exactly on political grounds, but on a very ingenious ground you take for your own purpose the argument used by my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), the ex-Minister of Justice, in reference to the Supreme Court of Canada. In this House of Commons there may appear to be some inducement to accept such a bill, but in the country at large and in the light of the statute, you cannot do what you propose. The law protecting judges was so written in a fundamental way that even on the income tax you could not touch them. In the statute of 1906, reproduced in the revised statutes of 1927 is section No. 29 just following section 28, which says:
(3) The salaries and retiring allowances or annuities shall be payable by monthly instalments, and the salaries and retiring allowances and annuities of the judges who are now by law entitled to receive the same free and clear of taxes and deductions imposed under any act of the parliament of Canada., shall continue to be paid free and clear of such taxes and deductions.
That meant that when they were appointed they had a salary fixed by statute, and no deductions could be made from that salary by any act of parliament. Are we to say now that a man seventy-five years of age is not fit to carry on as a judge? What if a son were to say to his father, "You are seventy-five years old now; you are too old to conduct your business. Get out of the store; I will take everything over." The father would say, "This belongs to me; I bought it and I am going to stay here." According to their contract with the state the judges can remain on the bench as long as they can discharge their duties properly, and it should be left to their

.Judges Act-Mr. Mercier (St. Henri)
own judgment to decide when they should retire. We name a man to the bench because he has a conscience; it cannot be otherwise. If he is unable to carry on beyond the age of seventy-five he will say, "I cannot discharge my duties according to the law and in fairness to the citizens who come before me." I should like to refer to section 2 of this bill, which says:
This act shall come into force on the first day of July, 1933, but in the case of any judge who, on the day when he attained the age of seventy-five years or on the first day of July, 1933, whichever is later, has held office for less than_ Sfteen years, the operation of this act shall in his case be postponed until he has continued in office for fifteen years, and shall thereupon have its full force and operation.
Thus a -man appointed at the age of sixty-two or sixty-five

and there have been a few such appointments-will go beyond the age limit of seventy-five. What will happen in his case? This clause as it stands cannot pass; it will do an injustice to those who must retire when they reach the age of seventy-five. Those who have not completed fifteen years on the bench will serve beyond the age of seventy-five and you will be keeping on the bench a judge who, according to your own words, is not fit. After he reaches the age of seventy-five we will be paying him 59,000, though you will be retiring those with greater experience who have completed more than fifteen years service. So I say if this section is passed in its present form it will work a grave injustice on those who are obliged to retire on reaching the age limit. In the case of Mr. Justice Mignault the exMinister of Justice (Mr. -Lapointe) simply said, " W ell, according to the sacredness of contract Mr. Justice Mignault is entitled to compensation; we will give him his full salary as a pension, since he is compelled to leave the bench at the age of seventy-five. So Mr. Justice Mignault is getting his full salary, and there are no deductions made from it by way of income tax or anything else, since a pension is not taxable.
We have a contract with these judges, and I think at first it would be well for the state to pay them their full salaries if they are to be retired. But during these times of distress and depression, when the finances of the state are so heavily burdened, why not postpone this bill for four or five years in order to have time to settle everything? Time is a great healer, and everything will work out eventually. In the meantime, why tax the people of the country in order to pay a new judge a salary of S9,000 while at the

same time we must pay the retiring judge a gratuity of $6,000? If that retiring judge has been twenty-five years on the bench he will receive $7,000, so that we will have to pay $16,000 instead of $9,000 in order to replace a man who may be quite able to carry on.

speechtext:
What about the interests of litigants, whose counsel has been presenting an argument? The judge, an hour and a half behind the argument, says, "What did you say"?
Mr. MERCIEiR: (St. Henri): But very often the lawyers are to blame; sometimes they are all mixed up in their arguments, and they have not their cases prepared. In addition it seems to me that we are interfering in provincial affairs. This does not apply to Quebec, because there the judges are not fortunate enough to be able to increase their salaries, but often in Ontario judges receive extra remuneration for giving extra service for the benefit of the province. Why should we say to a judge that if he sees fit to remain on the bench after the age of seventy-five he shall receive in salary only the amount of the pension to which he is entitled, and if he receives $1,000 from the province he will only receive $5,000 from the Dominion? speechtext: Hon. gentlemen should not laugh, because we are discussing a very important question. More than that, when people begin to laugh at the bench they are laughing at one of the corner stones of the nation.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the broad principle of retiring judges at the age of seventy-five is a debatable question. There is a large body of opinion which holds that at seventy-five, with the maturity and wisdom - that he has attained, a judge is perhaps more fit to discharge his duties on the bench than is the case with younger men. I believe the consensus of opinion throughout this country is that a judge should retire at the age of seventy-five, but if a judge of the federal court or of the county court should retire at that age there is no reason why a judge of the supreme court should not retire in the

Judges Act-Mr. Factor
same way. I should say, however, that the government is not accomplishing its object by this legislation. The Prime Minister just asked my hon. friend from St. Henri (Mr. Mercier) with reference to the judge who, after listening to an argument for an hour and a half, asks the lawyer, "What did you say"? I say that in all probability this same judge will accept the two-thirds of his salary to which he is entitled and will remain on the bench, so you will not succeed in the object you have in view.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: Then he will work for nothing.

speechtext: I do not think this legislation will meet the situation; these men who are supposed to be incapable of discharging their duties will continue to sit on the bench but will receive a lower salary.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: And if I know them well they will remain on the bench.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: I hate to acknowledge that parliament, because it is unable by constitutional methods to retire judges after they have reached the age of seventy-five, has to resort to a financial scheme or arrangement such as is proposed in this bill. I believe that the time has come when the broad question of amending our own constitution should receive the attention of parliament. If under present conditions we are unable to amend the act so as to pass legislation which will facilitate the retirement of judges, a principle in which I believe, it is high time that parliament adopted legislation to enable us to do that. I would ask the Solicitor General and the Prime Minister this question: How do the3' expect by this legislation to get rid of those judges who are incapable or incapacitated and therefore cannot attend to their duties? The mere fact that a judge is over seventy-five years of age should not be a reason for his being removed from the bench, but if by reason of age or infirmity he is incapacitated and is unable to discharge his duties, the procedure is provided by section 28 of the Judges Act, and you do not have to-

The Prime Minister says
that, under the old section 28, if after due inquiry a judge is found to be incapable by reason of age or infirmity his pay is reduced or cut off. In that case he goes off the bench.

No; he stays on if he
wants to.

speechtext:
Well, there will not be
many judges who will stay on without salary, whereas under this legislation you are retaining the judge and paying him two-thirds of his salary.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS

speechtext:
In other words, there will
be an incentive for the incapacitated judge to remain on the bench because he will get two-thirds of his salary. That is the net result of the legislation. The Prime Minister may laugh, but I should like him to meet that argument. Is there not an incentive for a judge, knowing that he will get two-thirds of his salary, to remain on the bench?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: If there is such an incentive it is itself an indication of the unfitness of the man to be on the bench.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
But there is nothing in
this legislation to remove him, and I submit that it is high time some method were evolved, whether by amending the British North America Act or by some other means, to go about this matter in a direct fashion under proper authority.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
Why did you not do
that in 1922?

You had the same right

speechtext:
The fact that it was not
done in 1922 is no excuse for adopting a method of camouflage now to give a judge two-thirds of his salary. I think the government should take into serious consideration the principle involved in this matter. I am thoroughly in agreement with the govern-men's intention of removing any judge who is incapable of discharging the duties of his office after the age of seventy-five. Further than that, I agree to the principle that every judge of the supreme court should retire at the age of seventy-five. I submit however that the proper method is not being followed.

Judges Act-Mr. Dupuis
The government are acknowledging that they are unable to do it by legislation, but they are attempting to do it by a cheap scheme. That is all it is-a cheap scheme which is tantamount to saying to a judge, " if you stay on the bench you will get two-thirds of your salary." The result will be however, as an hon. member suggests, that the scheme instead of being cheap may be expensive, because if the judge does not retire a new judge will have to be appointed and the additional salary will have to be paid.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I believe the intention of the government is sound so far as unfit judges are concerned, but it seems to me that this bill as it is drafted is too drastic. No door is left open to those judges who are still capable, and if there is one class of our Canadian society to whom we should do no injustice it is our judiciary. I have in mind judges in Montreal who are in the neighbourhood of seventy-five years of age or over and who are most capable, some of them being perhaps the best judges we have in the whole country. Now, what will happen? Not only will the judges affected by this bill be deprived of their salaries, which is a matter of comparatively small importance, but lawyers who are accustomed to plead before such judges will suffer, and most of all the people who seek redress before our courts; they will be deprived of the wisdom of such eminent members of the judiciary. If it were possible for me to name such judges I would name them, and I know that the Prime Minister and the members of this house would bear me out in that regard.
I do not quite understand how this government could bring in legislation of this sort in such an indirect way to attain an end which will never be reached. They will not get rid of unfit judges. There is section 28 of the act which, if the government were willing to apply it, would accomplish the same purpose, with this distinction, that the government by section 28 have the discretion to apply it to those who are unfit, either by reason of ill health or by infirmity or otherwise, leaving on the bench those judges w7ho are capable. May I here interject this parenthesis in answer to what the Prime Minister said, putting a question to the hon. member for St. Henri. He said, "What about those judges who, after listening to a lawyer for an hour and a half, ask him what he has said?" I may ask the Prime Minister whether in his experience as a lawyer he found that it was only those judges above seventy-five years of age to whom that remark could apply.

I did not hear the hon.
gentleman.

speechtext: I am asking the Prime Minister whether, in his experience as a lawyer, he has found that only judges above seventy-five years of age could suddenly ask him, after listening to him for an hour and a half, what he had said? subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS

would refer to the hon. gentleman himself as one of them.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before recess we were discussing the advisability of passing Bill No. 84, to amend the Judges Act. I contend that the aim the government is seeking to attain w7ill not be reached by this legislation. They say that they intend to oblige judges who are unfit to take their pensions, presumably they believe, from their experience, sometimes judges are bad judges of themselves, and although incapacitated by ill health or otherwise, they do not seem to realize the fact. That may be true. It is because of this that, I believe, in 1922 or thereabouts, this question was brought up in the house by the previous government and Senator Dandurand, presented an argument to that effect and piloted the discussion of the bill which is now on the statute book as section 28 of the Judges Act, chapter 105 of the revised statutes of Canada. The argument then advanced by Senator Dandurand w7as to that effect and cannot be applied as an argument in favour of the present bill, because the then administration was faced with the situation that some Canadian judges were repeatedly asking and obtaining leave of absence for six months. There was only one way to oblige them to take their pensions and that was to pass legislation to reduce their salaries to naught. But it applied only to those who were unfit, whereas the bill now before us applies to all judges who reach the age of seventy-five years.

Judges Acl-Mr. Dupuis
Is it necessary that I should remind the house of many instances not only in the judiciary, but in many other walks of life, of people over seventy-five years of age whose services the country is still pleased to retain? What would have happened in England during the time of Gladstone if they had applied to public men legislation such as this? Where is the Englishman who is not proud of what Gladstone did for his country even in his later years? What would have happened in Canada if such legislation had been applied to public men in the case of Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and many others who, on account of their experience and capabilities, were of immense value to this country? In the judiciary to-day, as I said before, we still have judges of advanced years who render eminent service to their country and their countrymen. Therefore I believe this legislation should either be amended or dropped; it is so drafted that it reaches the limit of despotism. The government will say to a judge: When you reach the age of seventy-five years, whether you are able, whether you have large experience, whether you are physically and mentally fit, you must get off the bench; we want to put a younger man in your place. That reminds me of a conference of United States medical men held in New York some years ago when one of them gave a lecture stating that every United States citizen who reached the age of seventy-five years should be put out of existence with strychnine or some other poison; that he was a nuisance to the people of that country. That gentleman was laughed at. One is not obliged to look with a searchlight to find in any land men who, after they reach that age, are still useful citizens.
The purpose of this bill is to retire on pension members of the judiciary after they have reached the age of seventy-five, by reducing their salary to the amount of their pension. The Prime Minister, with the gesture of an offended virgin, said: We have no political motive, and the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is not speaking by the book when he contends we have a political motive in the back of our heads. I am ready to admit, because the Prime Minister said so, that he has no political motive, but I would ask him and hon. members opposite: What is the motive? Although they know many members of the judiciary of seventy-five years of age or over are still rendering eminent service to their country, they are obliging them to retire against their willingness to [DOT]continue to fulfil their important duties. What
is the purpose of this legislation? It is to put younger men in their place, and I use the words of the Prime Minister. He does not want to name any judge over the age of sixty to any court. He wants to appoint younger judges. If it is not done from a political motive, the consequences at all events will be political in that when the judges reaching the age of seventy-five are retired, regardless of their capacity, the positions will be given to younger men, political friends who will stay on the bench for many, many years after this government has passed away.
I heard the hon. member for Quebec East use the argument that this is a breach of contract. I am of the same opinion. I believe that it is an absolute breadh of contract with these judges who have abandoned their practice as lawyers, and generally speaking they were lawyers with a good practice, and some of them derived from their practice much more than the salary of a judge. Through a high spirit of service to the country they gave up their practice to accept nomination as a judge, with the absolute assurance of a solemn contract that they would receive a certain salary, and that no one, not even the government, would be able to deprive them of such salary. If to-day the government by this legislation puts them out of office, where is the hon. member of this house who will not call that a breach of contract? It is a breach of contract to put out of office very capable judges in order to appoint younger men. And what will be the consequence? Will that save money to this country? Quite the contrary. The result will be that the judge who is pensioned will receive twodhirds of his salary, let us say $7,000 a year, and in some cases $6,000, and the new judge who will be appointed will receive $9,000 a year, so that every retirement will cost the country $16,000 a year. I therefore see no reason in the world why the government should insist on this legislation. It seems to me that in justice to those judges who are capable and in justice also to those who were at the head of the government when section 28 was passed, this government should have the courage to apply section 28 and use their discretion in putting out of office those who are really unfit and allowing to remain those who can efficiently perform their functions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of the principle of this bill. Having practised for a period of something like thirty-nine years, perhaps my opinion is worth something. What I do not like about this measure is what I might call the retro-

Judges Act-Mr. Jacobs

activity of it. Outside of that I think it is a very proper bill and it is carrying out the theory of the act which was passed in 1927, and for which we claim the credit I remember that immediately after the passing of that act in 1927 a judge of the Supreme court of Canada was retired, Mr. Justice Mignault, I believe. We omitted to provide for his pension, and that matter was not taken care of until the present government-

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
It was looked after by
the old government.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: Time flies.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
Yes, it always does.
I was always in favour of the scheme whereby pensions would be provided for judges retired in this particular way. Mr. Justice Mignault made the point that he was named under a contract mentioned in the statutes and that the government had failed to carry out the terms of the contract. In the present case, however, as I understand it, constitutional objections have been made and are recognized that the bill cannot go through as did the bill of 1927 because at that time we were dealing with federal courts, and the present bill, is a hang-over from the period prior to 1867 when we took over from the provinces the legislation affecting judges.
There is another objection that I see to a wholesale retirement of judges. Many of them have now reached the age mentioned in the bill. I should say that probably thirty or forty of them would be compulsorily retired under its provisions. That would amount to about a quarter of a million dollars for annuities for these judges. That is a tidy sum of money at the present time when we are casting about in every way to get money in order to carry on a hand-to-mouth existence. Just now I think it is a luxury which might well stand over until the years to come which we hope will be brighter than those we have gone through in the past three or four years.
Why should a judge be permitted to remain on the bench for more than the period allotted to men by the psalmist? Three score years and ten was considered to be the span of man's allotted life on this earth.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
And
then the Senate.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
The Senate is a horse of
another colour. We ought to give these judges time to prepare themselves for their Maker, and if they are on the bench every day rendering judgments, what chance have they when they go into the next world? I have a good 
deal of respect for the bench. I can speak a little more freely now than when I practised before them, but I also recognize that judges have their failings, and I think it will be generally admitted that a man under seventy-five years of age generally speaking is a better man than one over seventy-five. It is the most natural thing in the world that a man should have passed the zenith of his power previous to seventy-five years of age. Even in the days of Shakespeare it was recognized that a judge on the bench must be in the full vigour of physical and mental attainment. I think Shakespeare places the judge in the fifth stage of man's life: He talks of the justice.
In fair round belly with good capon lined,
With eyes severe, and beard of formal cut.
I have that beard of formal cut. But when he gets into the sixth stage he talks about-
. . . the lean and slipper'd pantaloon,
With spectacles on nose and pouch on side,
His youthful hose well saved, a world too wide
For his shrunk shank; and his big manly voice,
Turning again toward childish treble, pipes
And whistles in the sound.
That is the sixth stage. We wish to place all our judges in the fifth stage, so as not to have them in the condition which Shakespeare describes in stage six. After all, when a man is seventy-five years of age it does seem to me that $6,000 a year is a fair salary. Where could he get more than S6,000? It would be impossible. No doubt his family will have grown up. He has not the obligations that as a younger man he would have had. Altogether I think he ought to be satisfied with the smaller amount.
Another reason is that there are others trying to reach the bench. It is not fair or right that a position of such importance which is held out to eminent members of the bar who have worked and toiled upward in the night while others were enjoying life, should wait until the kindly hand of death removes the eminent judge. I do not consider it just to the other lawyers. What I do not like, however, is the wholesale appointment of thirty or forty men, all selected from one particular party at this particular time. The thing should be done with decency and decorum. It is not fair that such a thing should be perpetrated or practised upon the community just now.
Some suggestion was made during the debate about the eminence of learned judges, and that we would be deprived of their talents. Well,
I think we have men at the bar to-day who are as eminent as men found on the bench. I

Judges Act-Mr. Dupre
believe every one will agree with that. The Prime Minister referred to a case-I do not know whether it was hypothetical or actual -where a judge asked an attorney after listening. "What did you say?" or "What were you saying? I well remember a case in which I was engaged where, shortly after we returned from lunch we found that the judge was asleep on the bench.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: How old was he?

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: I do not know what his age was, but that did not interfere with his sleep.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: That is a good argument.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I put a question to the witness to which my opponent objected. There we were, with the judge snoring peacefully, waiting to see what would happen. Finally when we saw that the judge was not likely to awaken for some time I said, "Well, seeing that the question is not important I shall withdraw it." I lost my case. Whether it was because the judge merely had his eyes closed and was listening to me or whether he actually did not hear what I was saying, I do not know. However that is an experience which may happen to anyone.
We know the story of the Duke of Devonshire who, while addressing the House of Commons on one occasion, yawned. He provoked some amusement at the time, and when a friend met him outside the building and said, "Is it true, that you fell asleep or yawned when you were delivering your address?" the Duke replied, "Did you hear the speech?" The reply was "No." "Well, then," said the Duke, "if you had heard it you would have known why." Little things of that kind do not amount to very much, but they all go to show that as a person grows older his natural ability does not improve. It is a stage of decadence. We are simply doing by legislation what nature has done before. I see my good friend the Minister of Railways and Canals still shows a little interest in medicine, although he is now far removed from it-we have railroaded him out of it.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay
this legislation, but I have one or two observations to add. I do not believe it necessary to reply to the accusation made by the hon. members for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) to the effect that political motives are behind this legislation. That accusation is unfounded. The only motive behind this legislation is that of securing high efficiency in the administration of justice. We have also to think of the taxpayers and litigants who are complaining because efficiency is not at its highest point. Everything enacted in the bill has already been enacted by section 28 of the act, which is chapter 105 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927.
If I may say so, the present legislation is nothing but a sort of alleviation or mitigation of the drastic legislation enacted by section 28. Deprived of its legal phraseology section 28 enacts that any judge who by reason of age or infirmity is incapacitated or disabled from the due execution of his office shall cease to be paid. We say that any judge who has attained the age of seventy-five will, if he wishes to do so, continue to hold office, but he will not receive more than the annuity to which he would be entitled. That is all we say.

Salaries of judges in office after attaining the age of seventy-five years.
They are not retired, they are remaining in office at two-thirds of the salary. That to my mind is a most vicious distinction. Judges are going to remain in office, yet it was the only argument for the bill that judges incapable of carrying on their duties should retire. But you are not necessarily retiring these judges under the terms of this bill. The only effective result of this legislation is to perpetuate them in office, if they so desire, at two-thirds of the salary they are drawing now. So if a judge at the age of seventy-five has the faults imputed by the hon. member he still remains, and all the imperfections of the present system absolutely continue in existence. Here we are in these times of depression when we are reducing the salaries of small people, going to impose upon this nation an additional burden of $100,000 during the first year, with probably a progressive increase as the years go on. I think the principle of this legislation is absolutely futile. If the house were in favour of retiring judges compulsorily at the age of seventy-five that is an entirely different thing, because then we would get rid of any incompetency such as is alleged by the Solicitor General in regard to certain judges. But this legislation does not cure that situation.
In the second place it establishes what I consider the very iniquitous principle of differentiation between judges; those with full salary up to the age of seventy-five, and others with two-thirds, if they decide to remain in office after this bill becomes law. To my mind, it is, if not intentional, at least in effect an attack on the judiciary of Canada. It is introducing a principle of differentiation in regard to service, and I think it is a very dangerous principle. The legislation is only

speechtext: Supposing a judge has been appointed-and I believe there are a few cases of this kind-who, in order to complete fifteen years of service, will have to serve until he is more than seventy-five years of age. Why should there be a different kind of treatment in his case? If other judges are obliged to retire and take their pension at the age of seventy-five, or to accept a reduced salary if they remain on the bench, why should this newly appointed judge remain on the bench at his full salary until lie is seventy-seven or seventy-eight years of age?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: There is one case, I believe, in which the appointee was at an advanced age when he was appointed. He has no retiring allowance until he has served fifteen years, and he will be over seventy-five when he has served for that length of time. It is desirable to take care of that case, otherwise he would be retired with no annuity at all.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES AFTER ATTAINING AGE OF SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS
speechtext: But according to the arguments advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite this morning he will be seventy-five years old, and he will be no good. Surely the rule must apply to all or none.

The right hon. gentleman argued this morning that when a judge reached the age of seventy-five he should withdraw, being no longer qualified. Why should he be considered qualified if he has not served fifteen years by the time he reaches the age of seventy-five? If he is not fit to be a judge under those circumstances this should apply to everyone. If there is necessity for a special vote in one particular case, as my right hon. friend suggests, it would be better to have the house vote the salary to that one man. But why should we

Judges Act
embody in the law what is certainly a deviation from the principle expounded by my right hon. friend and by the Solicitor General?

I was careful to say that there might be doubts whether seventy-five should be made the governing age or not, hut as a matter of fact, in looking through the cases, I believe the department discovered that at least one judge-there may be another case, but in the hurry of work one cannot say- who would be past the age of seventy-five before becoming entitled to his pension. The purpose is to ensure that he does not lose his rights by reason of the fact that he was over sixty when appointed. I think, when we are making operative an act of this kind, it is desirable to protect the interests of a judge in such a case, because he is otherwise subject to all the provisions of the act. If he is infirm or disabled he can be dealt with under the provisions of the statute that refer to cases of that kind, but this clause is intended to meet this particular case.
Mr. M'K.ROI KR (St. Henri): My right hon. friend is trying to carry out the state contract with respect to this individual judge, making it possible for him to receive his pension. That is the position; you cannot get away from it. The endeavour is being made to respect his contract, affording that judge an opportunity to remain after the age of seventy-five years, so that he may obtain his pension. If this is done it will be a breach of contract, and if it is a breach of contract with respect to one judge or a few judges, the principle constitutes a breach of contract towards the other judges who have reached the age of seventy-five. The government might give to that judge, for the time he may have served over a period of thirteen years, a pension proportionate to the length of service he has rendered before reaching the age of seventy-five.
