subtopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS

speechtext: The house in committee on Bill No. 98, to amend the Post Office Act-Mr. Bennett -Mr. Gagnon in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
This bill has been
reprinted and the question propounded yesterday by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is now answered in the negative. This bill cannot apply to weekly newspapers because, first of all, it applies only when newspapers are transmitted for a greater distance than forty miles and then:
The newspapers and periodicals described in the immediately preceding subsection, upon any copies in excess of 2,500 copies, shall be subject to postage-[DOT]
At such and such a rate, and in any event the advertising medium in any weekly newspapers the officials have any record of, does not exceed 50 per cent.
I have secured answers to the questions asked by the leader of the opposition. The first is that newspapers coming from the United States to Canada, come in free. The postage is paid there and by international arrangement the papers come into this country. On our newspapers we pay the postage here and they go into the United States. In that country the zone system prevails with respect to advertising and the rate is ten cents a pound on the advertising portion, so that Canadian papers, so far as that .is concerned, do not meet with greater competition in that regard; that is, United States papers while coming in free, pay ten cents per pound on the advertising content as determined at Washington, plus the ordinary postage for the privilege of transmission.
The right hon. member asked whether this would affect the Saturday Evening Post. The
answer to that is no. The Saturday Evening Post is dealt with by the legislation of 1931, under which it will be recalled that that paper falls within the category that pays the five cents a copy to this country. The revenue derived from that last year was very substantial. I cannot give the exact amount but it exceeded five thousand dollars a month. The other question which the right hon. gentleman asked was whether this effected any change with respect to rates payable other than those he mentioned, namely, to increase the rate of four cents on the advertising content in excess of the present figure. There is no change in that regard in the statute as it now reads.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Customs Tariff Amendment

Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 93, to amend the customs tariff.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Gagnon in the chair.
On section 1-Rate of exchange on depreciated currency in computing value for duty of goods imported.
Would you mind reading the first sentence of subsection (9), Mr. Chairman?

It reads as follows:
"(9) (a) Notwithstanding the provisions of any other law, the governor in council may, from time to time and as occasion requires, order and direct, subject to such exceptions as may be made, what shall be the rate of exchange fixed for any currency in computing the value for duty of goods imported into Canada from any place or country the currency of which is depreciated, and in ease a sum in Canadian currency less than the invoice value of the goods in the currency of the place or country of export, computed at the rate of exchange so ordered, be paid for in goods, the actual selling price of the goods to the importer shall be regarded as less than the fair market value of the goods when sold for home consumption, and the provisions of this section shall apply and special or dumping duty shall apply equal to the difference between the value of the invoice computed at the current rate of exchange or at the average current rate from time to time fixed by order of the governor in council, and the value of such invoice, computed at the rate of exchange for duty so ordered as aforesaid, or may be less than such difference as the governor in council may from time to time order and direct; and the governor in council may order and direct that iii all cases of sales or consignments of goods imported into Canada, where the importer owns, controls or is interested in the business of the exporter, or the exporter owns, controls or is interested in the business of the importer, or the importer and exporter operate under a controlling or holding company, notwithstanding the expressed terms of the sale or consignment, the transaction shall be regarded as a sale and the actual selling price to the purchaser in Canada shall be taken to be the value of the goods in the currency of the place or country of export converted into Canadian currency at the current rate of exchange, or at the average current rate from time to time fixed by order of the governor in council, and shall be regarded as less than the fair market value of the goods when sold for home consumption, and the provisions of this section shall apply and special or dumping duty shall be deemed to apply equal to the difference between the value of the invoice computed at the current rate of exchange or at the average current rate from time to time fixed by order of the governor in council, and the value of such invoice computed at the rate of exchange for duty so ordered as aforesaid, or may be less than such difference as the governor in council may from time to time order and direct. .
[Mr Speaker.]
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

I should like to point
out that there is a typographical error in line 17, where the word "in" should be struck out and the word "the" substituted, so that it will read: "be paid for the goods." I move accordingly, Mr. Chairman.
Amendment agreed to.

May I ask the minister
what the clause that has just been read means?

If my hon. friend will
follow the section I think he will see that we have just put into words what the department has been doing since September when England went off the gold standard. We provided by orders in council for the exchange value of the pound for duty purposes. We provided also for the exchange value of the pound for special duty purposes. Then, as exchange was moving up and down, and as stability or an attempt at stability was desirable, we passed orders in council from time to time fixing the average value of the pound for special duty purposes. Having done that we found, and this appears in the section, that in order to avoid the payment of special duty, no matter what might be the exchange value of the pound, there were some who were selling at the fixed value of the pound for special duty purposes, thereby avoiding the payment of any special duty. There were certain articles of trade, such as wool, which had a gold value, and it was necessary for us to make orders in council in reference to the trade in wool. The trade in wines bottled in England, a trade which had been in existence for many years and was on a gold basis throughout the world, had to be provided for. These different movements and others, [DOT] if hon. members will accept this long sentence which is Gladstonian in its proportions, will develop just exactly the course of the department in handling the business. I hope that this lengthy explanation will be at least in a measure satisfactory.

Since the minister has stated that the object of the legislation is merely to put into statutory form a practice which has been followed by the department for some time, why is it necessary, if the practice was legal before, to put it now in the form of a statute?

That is of course a very proper question. When this was done in the first instance I was not in the country. I was in London, England, when gold took the flight. It was found that in an emergency in which quick action had to be taken a decision was

Customs Tariff Amendment
made which later had to be modified by order in council. Upon arriving home I canvassed the whole situation as carefully as I could. I was told, but not with emphasis, that the govenor general in council had done something which it had not authority to do. When I inquired what that w-as, I could not find out. However someone had set on foot the story that there was imperfection in the action taken by the governor in council, and in order to remove any possible doubt, I was anxious to effect a remedy. It is not proposed to go back and take the course of making merchants pay who have not paid but have been fair. The idea is to have the matter clear beyond peradventure. I may tell my hon. friend that the closest I could get to any definite statement as to what was done by the government which it had not power to do by order in council was that we had fixed an average for duty over fortnightly periods, and that it was necessary that the amounts so fixed should be the real exchange values of the pound on the particular dates. In order, as I say, to have some degree of uniformity we had fixed fortnightly values which obtained during the respective fortnights, action which it was suggested the government had not power to take. I think that it had. But if anyone wishes to challenge the action of the government I think this House of Commons, the final authority, ought to give the governor in council full power for what has been done.

Who was it
told the minister? Was it his colleagues?

No it was not. So far
as I know my colleagues are of the opinion that their action was correct. But there was the idea abroad to which I have referred. When I tried to localize it and find out what the trouble was the suggestion was made that we had not the power to fix the average value for duty covering fortnightly periods. So, in order to remove all possible doubt we are asking this House of Commons to pass this legislation, remembering, if you will, that it was necessary to act quickly. I think that while some people may object, in the main the action taken was beneficial to the country.

The minister admits that there was some doubt as to the legality of what was done in the past, since Great Britain went off the gold standard. Will he say now that this bill will regularize what was possibly done illegally in the past? Is it retroactive?

Yes. I say, as frankly as I can, that I believe the government had the authority. I believe that in the emergency the government should have had the power; I think all the chances are that it did. There is the view that improper or unwarranted action may be asserted. No one has done so thus far, but if such a contention should be advanced naturally the interests of the government and the revenue should be fortified. My answer to the hon. member would be that if this legislation is made retroactive from the month of September, when Great Britain went off the gold standard, we would be prepared for any threat on the part of any body in connection with the correctness of the action taken by the government.
Has any threat been made up to the present?
None that I know of.

No, that is not correct. The hon. member may have got that idea from what I said. But in connection with duty upon the pound, may I say that the value of the pound was fixed at par when our tariff was made. The value for duty is still with the pound at $4.86?. But there is a special duty, and that special duty is levied or was a short time ago, because at the present time there is none. The value of the pound for special duty was first $4.40 and then it was changed to $4.25. The exchange value of the day, or of this fortnightly period, deducted from $4.40 at first, and later from S4.25, constituted the special duty or what is commonly known as the dumping duty.
Would the minister tell us where in subsection (a) he finds authority for saying that the value for duty would be $4.86j? R states here that the value for duty is the value they fix.

That was in the order
in council, passed September 29, 1931, P.C. 2415.
What does it say?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, it is.

Customs Tariff Amendment

It says:
By order in council (P.C. 2415) dated 29th September, 1931, it is ordered that in computing the value for duty of goods imported into Canada from Great Britain, the rate of exchange shall be fixed at $4,861} to pound sterling being the par value thereof.

The section reads:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any other law, the governor in council may, from time to time and as occasion requires, order and direct, subject to such exceptions as may be made, what shall be the rate of exchange fixed for any currency in computing the value for duty of goods imported into Canada from any place or country the currency of which is depreciated, and in case a sum in Canadian currency less than the invoice value of the goods in the currency of the place or country of export, computed at the rate of exchange so ordered, be paid for in goods, the actual selling price of the goods to the importer shall be regarded as less than the fair market value of the goods when sold for home consumption, and the provisions of this section shall apply.

This legalizes that, if
there ever was any doubt as to its legality.
When the minister fixes the pound at $4.25-that is the power given him in the first fifteen lines of this section, is it not?
I would like to say that the minister does not fix the value, it is done by the governor in council.

Well when that is done,
when the value of the pound is fixed at $4.25, and then when they fix the average current value, the difference between those two shall be the dumping duty. Is not that the understanding? "And the first value fixed shall be the basis on which the value for duty is computed."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: But you have changed that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is what was expected, and that was why $4.40 was agreed upon by us all as being a fair price for the pound. It was expected that commodity values would rise about ten per cent; therefore, deducting ten per cent from $4.86 would give you some idea of what the value of the pound might be. As a matter of fact that was not exactly what happened. Perhaps the hon. member for North Waterloo has been reading the British trade journals. Nothing has been more surprising than the fact that instead of commodity prices rising with the depreciated currency, commodity prices actually decreased with respect to many basic commodities. There has been some increase during the last two weeks, but prior to that there was a steady decrease.

I have not checked it up,
but in one of the financial papers, I think the Financial Post of Toronto, the statement was made that commodity prices did increase to such an extent that the imposition of the dumping duty on the basis of $4.40 was entirely unnecessary, because the rise in commodity prices was sufficient to offset that depreciation. I have not checked it up, as I say, but certainly that statement is made by interested importers in this country.

The minister has just read
an order in council authorizing him to do certain things which he has been doing for the last two years. Now he says some doubt has arisen as to the legality of those things, and he brings in a bill to legalize what he has been doing.
No, it is to remove any chance of doubt. In my own mind I think council had ample authority to do what was done.
Then the minister wants this bill to contain ample justification for everything that was done, but it does not contain anything that would justify the order in council he read.
Carried.

No, it is not carried. I
may say that I have received complaints about this regulation-, and I should like to read a portion of a letter I received from a broker. Referring to another letter he had written he said:
My letter does not start with parliamentary language but expresses the exasperation felt by the vague meaning put into many of these regulations. It is quite possible there is a bidden meaning and I would suggest you ask that tliis resolution be explained.
This gentleman says he cannot find any meaning in the resolution and suggests that there may be a hidden meaning. I have read the resolution carefully, sentence by sentence, and I cannot find any hidden meaning at all; if it is hidden it is well hidden. I even read it backwards, and it makes just as much sense that way. Will the minister explain just what he means by a country whose currency is depreciated? Does he mean depreciated in terms of gold, in terms of American dollars, or in terms of Canadian dollars?
Currency is depreciated when it is at less than its recognized par throughout the world.
In terms of gold?

There might be a country where they traded jack-knives.
TMr. Ryckman.]

That is a sharp answer. I have here the Commercial Intelligence Journal for May 6, showing the value of different currencies. I find that on that date the United States dollar was worth 88 cents in gold and the Canadian dollar was worth 74 cents in gold. Now I want to ask the minister whether United States currency would come under this clause. That currency is depreciated in terms of gold, but it is above par in Canadian money; the United States dollar is worth about SI.13 in Canadian money. Would United States currency be considered depreciated under this clause?
No.

Let us see how this will work out. If this applies to -a country whose currency is depreciated in terms of gold but is still above Canadian currency, any advantage or supposed advantage which that countiy might derive from the depreciation of its currency would be more than offset by the further depreciation of the Canadian currency. In a case like that I ask the minister how he would justify the application of this section.
If the currency is at a premium of course the section would not apply.
I want to know whether that means at a premium in terms of Canadian money or in terms of gold. Here is a currency that is at a premium in terms of Canadian money and at a discount in terms of gold.

In the money market of Canada we have listed the currencies and their values; some are depreciated and some are appreciated, and we govern ourselves accordingly. The banks furnish the department, at eleven o'clock in the morning, the exchange rate in respect of any currency regarding which information may be asked.
I take it the minister means depreciated in terms of Canadian money. What will he do with respect to a country whose currency is above ours?
Frankly, I do not understand the question.
I want to know how the section will be made to apply.
The section does not apply.

Then I will ask this question. The United States is such a country: if we are buying goods from the United States does any currency dumping duty apply?

Customs Tariff Amendment

No, not when their
currency is at a premium.

Then will the minister explain this. I have here an appraiser's note for a small collection on an electric lamp. The appraised value-not the invoice value- is SI.90; United States exchange 26 cents; advance for duty, 72 cents, making a total value for duty of 82.88. How is that value for duty arrived at?
That has nothing to do with the section under consideration.

I think it has quite a bit to do with it. I will ask this question, then. If an American exporter is sending goods into Canada, with the Canadian dollar quoted at 88 cents American funds, and he offers to take the Canadian dollar at par, -what action will the officers take?
I do not know either that that question relates to this section. We require the United States money to be converted into Canadian value.
Will the minister say he will or will not impose a dumping duty equal to the difference in the currency?

It depends upon the manner in which payment is made. It must be the fair market value in the country from which the goods are imported and must have relation to our own currency, and if an American exporter takes Canadian money when the United States money is at a premium we charge the duty in that case.

Then the minister is charging the currency dumping duty against the United States as wtell ias against other countries whose currency is at a premium. I can recall a report that appeared in the newspapers some time ago of a speech of the Prime Minister in which he seemed to resent the fact that Americans did not give us 100 cents for the dollar. But if the American did offer full value the Minister of National Revenue would not let him do it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, no.
He said so.

We insist on the fair market value for duty purposes. If someone tries to charge less we step in in the interests of the business of the country and insist upon a fair market value, and the transaction is carried out on that footing.

It amounts to this. You simply say to the American, "You must not
give Canada one hundred cents for her dollar." Let us see what the section says in line 30:
... in all cases of sales or consignments of goods imported into Canada, where the importer owns, controls or is interested in the business of the exporter, or the exporter owns, controls or is interested in the business of the importer, or the importer and exporter operate under a controlling or holding company, notwithstanding the expressed terms of the sale or consignment, the transaction shall be regarded as a sale and the actual selling price to the purchaser in Canada shall be taken to be the value of the goods in the currency of the place or country of export converted into Canadian currency at the current rate of exchange, or at the average current rate from time to time fixed by order of the governor in council, and shall be regarded as less than the fair market value . . .
Leaving out the second clause we find this. If a certain relationship exists between an importer in Canada and an exporter in Britain, then the goods shall be regarded as being sold at less than fair market value and the dumping duty shall apply. Is that what the minister intends to say?

I intended to say what
the hon. member has read.

The minister intends to
say this, that if a partnership or relationship of principal and agent exists between an exporter in England and an importer in Canada, then the goods shall be regarded as being dumped and as being sold at less than fair market value. Is that what the minister intended?

Yes, with this addedif the price is the value for special duty, because some have been evading the special duty. How? By using in the transaction the value that has been fixed as the value of the pound for special duty, so that there is no special duty payable at all. In some cases they have been willing to pay the merchant in England a higher price than they needed to pay him, in order to evade paying the special duty in Canada. If I have an affiliated company in England and if I am prepared to pay at a higher rate than the currency exchange rate I am simply taking money out of one pocket and putting it into the other and not giving the government its fair share of duty.

Where is that contained
in the bill? As I read it all that is necessary is that a certain relationship shall exist, that there be a partnership, and if they are partners, regardless of everything else, the dumping duty applies. That is the way I understand the bill.
Customs Tariff Amendment

If the invoice shows
that it would be a case of dumping if they were not partners.
Where is that in the bill?

The hon. member read
it; I do not wish to read it over again.

I cannot find it. I do not know who drafted the section, but here are 466 words all in one sentence, and for the life of me I cannot find the subject or the predicate of it. I do not know who drew it up.

I didn't think it was
quite as bad as all that.

It is, for I have actually
counted the words, and they are all in one sentence. The man who did it must have been working by the mile.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He must have been a
free trader.

A correspondent suggests
to me that there may be a hidden meaning in it. It has been said that language was given man as a means of concealing his thoughts; evidently that was the idea in the mind of the person who drafted this section. I suggest to the minister that he break it up into a number of clear, terse, concise sentences. When you want to draft a thing like this there are two principles to be observed: first, keep clearly in mind what you want to say and, secondly, say it.
Did my hon. friend ever think of applying that to himself?

I do the best I can. The
minister wants to say several things here. If he will tell us what they are, we will try to say them for him. The first thing he wants to say is that the governor in council shall have power td fix the values of certain currencies. Why not say that in one sentence and stop there? Then make another sentence for the next thing the minister wants to do. He wants to say that the value for duty shall be based on the value of currency so fixed. Let him put that in another sentence. Then he can have another saying that the governor in council shall have power to determine every fortnight the average value of the currency in question. Let him have another sentence stating that in case the actual price paid for the goods at the average current rate of exchange is less than the value for duty so fixed, the goods shall be considered as dumped and shall be liable to dumping duty. Then he can have another sentence saying that when certain relationships exist between 
the importer and the exporter the transaction shall be considered as a sale and values shall be determined as in the former clauses of the bill. Let him put those different ideas in different short, terse sentences expressed in simple words. Then we shall understand the matter and be able to discuss it intelligently. At present the bill does not make sense.

The Department of
Justice revised this section, and they did not have any difficulty with it. I must say I did not at first understand it as fully as I might have wished, but after reading it the second and third times, for I have read it a few times, I think it is plain. I do not believe my hon. friend would have to read it three times to understand it.

If the Justice department
drafted it they may be quite capable of understanding it, and the minister may also be capable of understanding it, but it has to be understood by ordinary mortals in business and they do not seem to know what it means. Even the officials of the department do not seem to understand it. I suggest that it be put into simple language so that the man in the street, even the hon. member for Weyburn may understand it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If they all understand it as well as he does, there will be none who do not understand it.
Carried.

No. We want it redrafted.
Does the minister not think it should be redrafted and simplified?

Frankly, I think not.
The difficulties have been caused by the complications in the working out of business, the fluctuations we have had; by reason of changes in exchange values a dumping duty may be shown one day and none the next. It is these things that cause difficulty, but anyone in the trade who will follow it, will understand it. I can appreciate the fact that a layman might find some difficulty on reading this over for the first time, but I think a bright minded person, on reading it the second time, would understand it fully.

Unfortunately we are not
all sufficiently bright minded to do so. In spite of what the minister says, in the last section I read where certain relationships are supposed to exist between the importer and the exporter and I cannot find in the bill anything other than that if such relationship exist, the goods are dumped no matter what

Special War Revenue Act
the price is. Surely the minister ought to be willing to clear this up by clarifying his language.
I think it is clear now.

Mr. Chairman, you have
been proceeding so rapidly that perhaps I have missed the clause concerning which I should have liked to make some observations. If you would permit me I should like to make them now. It was with regard to a debate of about a week ago in connection with the tax on corporations. Am I in order?

Yes.

Income War Tax Act

I said at the time that the
removal of the $2,000 exemption on corporation incomes has created a discriminatory-position so far as small corporations are concerned. May I repeat, lest I be misunderstood, that I am not objecting in any sense to corporations paying income tax. My objection is based entirely on the disproportion between the tax paid by a business which happens to be incorporated as compared with the-
Carried.

If hon. members say it is
carried before I am through, it will take all the longer. There is a disproportion between the tax paid by the incorporated company and that paid by a similar business which happened to be owned by one or two persons. I object to the great difference in the taxation. I take as an example the tax which has to be paid by a corporation having a profit of $5,000 as compared with the tax on the $5,000 profit earned by a private individual. As I said at that time the amounts payable were in the one case something like S713 and in the case of the private individual only about $120. My contention was that the difference was entirely too great. The minister attempted to meet my statement by saying that I had not allowed for salaries. I want to say now that I did allow for salaries. When I spoke of the $5,000 income I presumed that salaries had been paid, and I omitted the actual computation as far as salary was concerned1. Salary having been omitted in both cases in my computation the result was almost exactly identical in each case. If a profit-and I am speaking of a net profit in either case-is $5,000, and for the purpose of argument we want to say that in each case the manager of the concern receives a salary, the joint stock company at a salary of $3,000 and the manager of the private business on an allowance, if ybu wish to call it that, of $3,000, the difference, if it is computed by way of a tax on the company and by way of individual taxation, is, if we care to take it that way, $919 to be paid by the corporation or its owner by way of individual taxes, and only $346.50 to be paid by the private owner. I am trying to point out that the difference is entirely too great. I am not objecting to the principle of taxation of the corporation, but it seems unnecessary to state that it is utterly unfair that a business which shows a net profit of, we will say, $5,000 on capital should have to pay $919 while a privately owned business making a net profit of $5,000 pays only $340.50. I have checked these figures carefully, and they represent the difference between the two amounts in the case to which I referred the other day when it was taken for granted that I had not included salaries-$572 in one case and $593.75 in the other, or a difference of only $21.75.
I should like, not for the purpose of delaying the committee but to point out what I regard as an absolute injustice, for a few moments to review the situation. I think when the jncome tax was first introduced so far as corporations were concerned, in order to avoid double taxation, after the company had paid its taxes and the shareholders had received their dividends, they were allowed to deduct some eight per cent on individual receipts because of the fact that the company had already paid taxes on that income. It was regarded as unjust that taxation should be paid twice on the same sum. I believe that is a sound principle and if I cared to look back I could quote the present Prime Minister as having said what I am now saying, namely that, the principle of double taxation is unsound. I could mention a good many members on the opposite side of the house who took that position. Following that I believe it was the late Hon. Mr. Robb who removed the provision for the eight per cent allowance, but included a provision for a family corporation. That has been removed by the minister. In fact, the minister has done these three things within a very short period: He has removed the exemption which joint stock companies enjoyed; he has removed the family corporation provision, and he has increased the rate of taxation.
Just to make the comparison still more glaring may I point out that the owners of a joint stock company have to pay from four to seven income taxes on the same sum of money. The exemption of eight per cent has been abolished. We now have, first, a tax of twelve and a half per cent on the corporation, which is paid by the company itself. The individual is then taxed on the balance which he draws in dividends. There is double taxation. He is then taxed on last year's tax, because that sum cannot legally be deducted. The municipality-and especially is this so in the province of Ontario-then charges him an income tax on the same income, and usually charges about twice as much as it ought to charge, because the tax is based on the mill rate or the assessment rate, and the assessments in most of our towns and villages are usually half or less than half the actual real estate value. The result is that the tax rate or the mill rate is perhaps
Income War Tax Act

forty mills where it ought to be only twenty, if assessments were properly made. So he has a municipal income tax on the same sum of money. Then, in my province along comes the provincial government, placing another tax on joint stock companies of one per cent of their capital. There are at least four income taxes paid by a man who happens to have his money invested in a joint stock company.
But* the point I wish to make-ijnd I have no hope that I will be successful in convincing the minister-is that in the case of the small company where there is a proprietor, or two or three proprietors in a family, on so small a profit as S5,000 a tax of over $900 is paid. That figure must compare with the S300 paid by the private individual. Let us take the figures which the minister mentioned the other day when he endeavoured to show I had not allowed for the $3,000 salary. Let me take the S3,000 salary in the case of a joint stock company which I had credited with a profit of $5,000. That reduces the profit to $2,000. Figure it out in that way. Even the small company which has a profit of only $2,000, a company which may be owned by one person or perhaps by one man and members of his family, pays a tax of more than $300, whereas his competitor next door pays only $120. My whole argument is to make this point, that the difference is entirely too great. I am not objecting to the corporation tax, but I do not see any reason wrhy the small man because he happens for convenience to have his business in the form of a stock company-and he gets his charter from the provincial government, not this government, and the provincial government taxes him-should be penalized by having to pay three times the tax on his profits that the man who does business the other way has to pay. I think it is wrong and should be corrected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Whether that be regarded
by my hon. friend as a satisfactory reply or

not, it is the only reply I can give, and it would not be fair to encumber the record by repeating the same argument.
With respect to his second objection, I am very largely in agreement with him. There is no doubt that the feature of double taxation is in itself objectionable. If conditions were fairly normal we might have eliminated it, but I must point out that now is not the time when we can consider such a proposal. When we do approach more prosperous conditions we ought, if possible, to get away from the feature of double taxation, not only in connection with the income tax but other taxes I might cite. Further we should try if at all possible, when conditions improve, to get away from the retroactive feature which has been present in the income tax since its inception, because it is very hard on an individual who has to pay a tax this year at an increased rate on an income which he received and spent last year, and possibly this year he may have no income. There are actual cases of that character. That is a hardship which we ought at the earliest possible moment to attempt to eliminate.
As far as triple taxation is concerned, first by the dominion, second by the province and third by the municipality, in connection with income tax, I am in accord with the views expressed by my hon. friend. I stated to the house, on Friday I think it was, that that subject came up for discussion at the last provincial conference, and as a result there is a committee of the higher officials of the provinces and the dominion at work at the present moment. I hope that as a result of their efforts we may arrive at a working basis which will be fair to the different taxation authorities and also to the individuals concerned.

I wish to bring to the minister's attention again the question of reinstating the exemption of $2,000 for small companies. I wish to back up what the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has just said in connection with this matter. Even to-day I received a telegram from the Charlottetown board of trade saying:
Incorporated companies here and council board trade urge reinstatement exemption of two thousand dollars to incorporated companies in budget.
They seem to think it is working a very great hardship on the small companies. I really think the minister should give serious consideration to this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not a complete answer I will admit, but I may say to my hon. friend that neither in the United States nor Great

Supply-Miscellaneous
Britain do they give any exemption whatever. If the small company feels itself aggrieved, particularly the type of company referred to by my hon. friend from North Waterloo, it is a simple thing to dissolve the company and pay the straight income tax. Admittedly the exemption was dropped for the purpose of enlarging the return to the treasury.
I cannot see that there is any injustice, as the exemption follows all along the line with every company.

Mr. Chairman, the exemption of $2,000 means a great deal to a little company that makes only $3,000 or $4,000 profit, whereas to a company making half a million it means nothing at all. What I am objecting to is the discrimination, and no matter how difficult it may be to raise revenue and how necessary it may be, I think the principle of justice and absence of discrimination should apply.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 9, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Mr. Bennett-Mr. Gagnon in the chair.
That it is expedient to amend the Tariff Board Act, chapter 55 of the statutes of 1931, to provide that the salary of the chairman shall be $15,000 per annum; and that any member of the board who has served for a period of ten years, and is, on completion of such period, of the age of sixty years or over, may be granted an annuity equal to one-half of the annual salary of such member.

Several members of the committee have already voiced their opinions in regard to this measure, and I wish ;o add my protest to the passing of the resolution. It seems to (me an extraordinary thing, that this resolution should be brought in at this time. It was only a few months ago that parliament decided what was to be paid the different members of the board. We
rMr. Spencer.]
have waited nearty three years to get the tariff board established, and these three years have been years in which a tariff board, if it was to be of service at all, should have beer, functioning. The real work of a tariff board has been done. Before the government undertook to revise the tariff in the drastic manner ft has, it would have been well advised to have had a board of competent persons to give advice not only with regard to our own domestic tariff but also with respect to questions such as those which arose at the recent conference of the governments of the British Empire. The government would have been well advised if they had had a tariff board to which they might have referred, for consideration and information, many matters that came up at that conference, and with regard to which they should have been advised before acting so hastily.
So far as one can see at the moment, the one purpose the tariff board is now intended to serve is in all matters referred to the board to keep the protectionist element in the tariff. The legislation is on trial; the board itself is on trial; the chairman of the board so to speak, is on trial. As yet, none of us knows how successful he may prove to be as the chairman of the tariff board. We do know that he has been on the bench for less than three years, and that in the exercise of his functions as a judge he appears to have given entire satisfaction; but how successful he may be as the chairman of a board concerned with commercial and industrial problems remains to be seen. Had the board been in existence for a few years, had there been opportunity to test its worth and the capacity of the chairman, then it seems to me the government might have been justified if necessary in asking parliament to grant some additional amount to the chairman, having regard to the services he was rendering. Up to the present, however, no services have been rendered; yet we are asked, on the very day on which we have been reducing the salaries of the judiciary, to give one member of the judiciary, who was among the junior members, a position which is incomparably beyond that which any of his former fellow members of the judiciary enjoy.
This morning it was decided that no matter how competent certain members of the bench might be, how considerable their service, they were to have their salaries reduced after they had reached a certain age, whether they were to carry on or not. They were to receive an annuity amounting to a stated sum. Their salaries and annuities, however, were not to be at all comparable to what the chairman of this board will receive. I understand that his salary is to be equivalent to that of the Chief

Tariff Board Act
Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, and that after ten years of service he is then to receive an annuity of $7,500 which is practically equal do the salary he was enjoying as a judge of the superior court.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He was getting $9,000, and $1,000 from Ontario, which made $10,000.

I thank the Prime Minister for the correction. However, it would appear that this gentleman certainly is receiving in salary and annuity, consideration away beyond that which is being given to members of the judiciary generally.
I want to give a further reason for declining to support this resolution, which indeed I strongly oppose. I told the Prime Minister at the time the legislation was being introduced that the Liberal party could not undertake, if it came into office, to continue the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to the tariff, and in so far as the tariff board is to be an agency to perpetuate the protective feature of the tariffs which have been put into force by the present government, we on this side must decline to be a party, either directly or indirectly, to anything of the sort. I say that much by way of a further reason for my being opposed to granting this very large salary to the chairman of the board.
May I give another reason. We were assured that the tariff board when appointed would comprise gentlemen whose names would commend themselves to the house as those of non-partisans-gentlemen who would be in every way acceptable. Well, the appointees, so far as one can judge at all, are all gentlemen who have been pretty faithful supporters of the Conservative party, including even one member who sat with the Progressive group in this house.
Oh, no.

Oh, yes; he has; I can give his record if my hon. friends want it. I do not think he ever supported, except when a decision of His Honour the Speaker was being challenged, a single motion that originated from this side of the house in opposition to the present government. We are now asked calmly to vote a salary of $15,000 per annum for ten years to the chairman of the board, and large salaries to the other members of the board, and then a pension for the rest of their lives at a sum equal to that of a judge of the superior court, notwithstanding the gentlemen who are on the board have been placed there for ten years by hon. gentlemen opposite and that they are 53719-3054
all, from their point of view as expressed: heretofore, politically opposed to the policies which we on this side have been supporting. That is asking a little too much of an opposition, or even of human nature, and we on this side cannot think of supporting the proposed resolution or any act based upon it.
It does seem extraordinary that after a great part of the time of the session has been taken up in reducing the salaries of civil servants, reducing the allowances of war veterans, reducing the indemnities paid to members of parliament, giving reasons why staffs must be cut down here and staffs cut down there, we have had within the last few days one man after another, especially persona grata to the Prime Minister and the government, being given salaries far exceeding those of the highest offices in the public * service. Just at this time, that kind of thing does more to create unrest than any other single action of the government. Those who have had their salaries cut down, war veterans who are expected to take less in the way of pensions, those who are obliged to make additional payments on income tax account, taxpayers generally, are all to-day comparing their position with that of those few favoured gentlemen who at this time are receiving special treatment at the hands of the government. We ought to oppose very strongly such exceptional cases, especially where there are not grounds sufficient to support them.

I should like to support the leader of the opposition in his protest against what I must regard as discriminatory treatment. I believe in paying good wages and salaries; I believe government employees or those who receive government appointments should be properly taken care of, but during this session and, in fact, for the last few years we have had what has been termed a policy of economy and under that policy there has been a cutting down of salaries affecting especially the lower paid people. There has been no gradation in this matter, but we have had a ten per cent cut all along the line. This has meant a great' deal of hardship. In additioh, staffs have been cut and many people have been thrown out of work altogether. I think it was only jmsterday that some of us were pleading that the rights of railway employees should be protected at this time; that they should not. be turned out on the street. The government would not listen to our pleas and put through legislation that we thought was designed in the interest of the bondholders, without paying any regard whatever to the employees of the railways. We have recently had to pass measures which lay a very heavy tax upon

the people of this country. When I think of families that to-day are Struggling to maintain the very minimum of a decent living, it seems to me absolutely wrong that such high salaries should be paid to certain individuals in the service.
I am not at all sure that it was necessary to get a judge to act as chairman of the board, nor that legal training is the best for the man who occupies that position. I can understand that legal training may be very necessary for certain positions, but it remains to be seen whether it is a good training for men who are placed in what might be termed executive positions or those involving considerable independent research. I am inclined to think a scientific training would be much more desirable than a legal. There are many men who have had practical experience as well as academic training who, I am sure, would be very glad to accept this position at a lower figure than that which is being offered.
Of course there is the larger question of the wide spread in our salaries. I think we should be tending towards a greater equality instead of a still wider spread. The suggestion has been made that the gentleman who has been appointed to this high position not only has special qualifications, but is also doing this as a matter of duty. I would like to think, if that is the case, he might be prepared to do his duty without receiving such very high emoluments for so doing. There are people who are doing perhaps less responsible work but are none the less doing their duty, who are being paid a wage or salary that is lower than would enable them to maintain anything like a decent standard of living. When I think of those high salaries, I remember that they are possible simply because of the taxation which is levied on the great mass of the people and which falls most heavily on some of the poorer people of this country. As one who for many years has come into contact with the poor people of Canada, I must protest against this further extension of this principle which we are asked to make to-night. I do not think it is at all necessary. I do not think any good explanation has been given why so soon after the original act was passed there should be an increase in salary.
I know it is possible for the Prime Minister to say that only by giving very high salaries can he secure the best men. I do not think that can be very well proven. I know it has been said that only by providing very fully for pensions 'can men be induced to give up more secure jobs. I do not think that contention has been or can be proven. I repeat: It seems to me at this time, when through

our taxation and otherwise people are being called upon to make great sacrifices, the example should be set by some of those who are occupying high positions in the service.

I feel I would be recreant to my duty if I did not protest against this resolution at this time. When the Tariff Board Act was passed, we understood that a salary of 112,000 was to be paid to the chairman of the board, and at that time it seemed to me and to people throughout the country that this was a pretty fair salary. Now we find that the intention is to increase it to
515.000,	which is more than judges are paid in any of the courts of this country and equal to what the Prime Minister of Canada receives. I can see no justification for increasing the salary to that extent. I believe he is worth being paid a fair salary, but it seeims to me that when you raise that to $15,000 a year, you are going beyond what is reasonable. We have been going through times of great stress; men as efficient in their respective callings as the chairman of this board has been in his are working for very small salaries or remuneration and can see no particular hope for the future. The poor people of this country are again being penalized by heavy taxation at a time when the number of persons on relief has increased by hundreds of thousands, until to-day, I am told, it stands at

principle cannot be carried out in the case of these higher officers. Conditions in this country are most serious and it is impossible for us to pay annuities on terms such as this resolution calls for when it must be done at the expense of the ordinary working man through imposing taxes on the things he consumes, such as sugar and boots and shoes, and so forth. I can see no justification for the last part of the resolution at all. The men who are appointed to this board from the chairman down are bettering their position through their appointment, and if they are not able to provide for their future through the greater salary they are receiving, I do not believe it is the duty of the poor people of Canada, the consumers, the farmers, and working classes, to provide for their future in addition to giving them this substantial remuneration during their first ten years of office. On behalf of the constituents I represent I protest as strongly as I can against the whole spirit of the resolution before the committee.

I believe, Mr. Chairman, that it is high time that the people of this country took stock of what is being done here and took serious note of the high salaries and remuneration that are being handed out just like a free gift to many of our-yes-public employees. It may interest the house to know that since the present administration came into power under the present Prime Minister numerous increases have been given to certain high officials, increases which have only been obtained by other employees in the civil service after many years of faithful service. I have before me a list of some of the increases that have been put into effect, I am told, under the Prime Minister. Some of them are very striking, and I will say almost alarming.
I find that the salary of Major General A. D. McNaughton, chief of the general staff, has been increased from 88,000 to 810,000. He receives the salary of a deputy minister. The Deputy Minister of National Defence, Colonel LaFIeche, appointed recently, gets another
810,000.	The man who was superannuated to make room for Colonel LaFIeche got $10,000 only after being in the service since 1879. Some of these new appointees are being given the same salary as those who are now being superannuated after years of faithful service to their country. Mr. Breadner, commissioner of customs, got one-third of the previous salary of the deputy minister, two other men being appointed, one as commissioner of excise and another as commissioner of income tax. The deputy got $10,000 after many years'
service. Mr. Breadner was given $10,COO as commissioner of customs, and now he has received an increase of $2,000.
I go right down the list and I find the most striking example in the Department of the Interior, where a man sixty-five years of age was superannuated, I am told, at $5,000 or $6,000, and another man who was away down in the civil service list was raised to the post of deputy minister at a salary of $8,000, and this new appointee I am told is seventy-two years of age. That to me requires a lot of explaining. That position is now costing the people of this country $14,000 because the man who was superannuated gets $6,000 or $7,000, and the man who was appointed in his place gets $8,000.
Commissioner Starnes of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police after forty years' service gets $6,450. Major General MacBrien who took his place gets $12,000 right off, and this in a time of stress when every government is preaching economy, and when this government is giving notice to every provincial government to cut down on its expenditures and to economize and to keep within its budget.
I listened very attentively to the Prime Minister's explanation this afternoon of this increase, and candidly I was not at all impressed by his explanation. My own interpretation as to the reason of the increase of salary is this, and I give it for what it is worth: that Judge Sedgewick was pretty well satisfied with his $12,000 until he saw the other two appointees who were getting $10,000, and after seeing them he said to himself: "Well, if these two men are worth $10,000 each per year I certainly am worth at least $15,000." I may be wrong but that is my own plain interpretation of this resolution. I know that there are members on the other side of the house who have gone about this country saying that God has appointed the Prime Minister in this time of crisis, but I also know that in the Scriptures we read of great trials and tribulations that are going to be sent in the latter days, and perhaps the Prime Minister is one of these.
The most serious thing in this whole proposal is the superannuation or annuity that it is proposed to give. By what right should any man after holding a good job at a good salary for a few years burden the people of this country with providing him with a life pension? Take even the ordinary members of that board. After five years' service they may get one-fifth, and after ten years' service one-quarter, of their salary. I say that this thing ought to stop. These life pensions should be cut out. I think also the whole
Tariff Board Act

system/of higher salaries for the higher officials in the government service should be carefully reviewed. Personally I am absolutely opposed to handing out a pension for a few years' service to anyone who has the gift of a good position. I feel sure if applications had been called for these positions so many would have been received that it would have been a great .task even to read them. Applications would have come readily from men of ability who would have been willing to take the job, not only as chairman but as members of the board at the amount received as indemnity by members of parliament. But the fact that he is given a pension for life, after having been given the gift of a job, is atrocious. It is just about time this sort of thing was stopped. Personally I am absolutely opposed to it. There are instances where the country in recognition of long and faithful service has given a gratuity or life pension. But where a man has been given a good job with a pension provision, under which he will receive one-fifth of his annual salary if he retires after a period of five years, I must express my indignation, especially when the burden falls upon the people of Canada, the majority of whom are not able at the present time to obtain the necessities of life. Personally I am opposed to the increase.

I shall state very briefly
my objection to this resolution. The arguments against it have already been well stated by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the hon. members for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) and New Westminster (Mr. Reid). I believe it my duty, however, to register a protest on behalf of my constituents. I believe I am not presumptuous when I say that in speaking for my constituents I voice the sentiments of all people of Manitoba, even if hon. members representing Manitoba constituencies do not feel called upon to speak upon this occasion.
So far as I am concerned there is no reason to doubt the ability of the man who has been chosen as chairman of the board. Some of us had the privilege, the honour or whatever you may call it, of meeting the board a few days ago. We came away with the impression that the chairman of the board was a man well qualified to fill the position. It was the first opportunity we had had to estimate his ability. That is not true of some other members of the board with whom we had been associated for a number of years and with whose ability and
fMr. Reid.]
capacity we were familiar. I say we have no reason to doubt the ability of the man who will discharge the functions of the office of chairman. But he would have occupied a higher position in the opinion of the people of Canada had he not, before entering upon the duties of his office, demanded this additional salary. We take it-and if I am wrong I shall gladly accept correction, so that we may know Where the responsibility lies- that he refused to accept the office unless the salary was increased.
Some years ago we used to talk about conscripting men for service. Sometimes we hear the term to-day, and we like to see men willing to serve their country. The chairman of this board would have stood much higher in the estimation of the Canadian people if he had been willing to serve without demanding the extra remuneration. There is no need of repeating the arguments which have been advanced-the difficulties of the times, the hardships which men are enduring, the tremendous loss suffered by the farmers, labouring classes, many of the smaller business men, and even larger business men. All these have suffered during the past few years. There is no necessity of recounting these facts; at such a time as this an increase of salary is simply without any justification whatever. I am amazed at the Prime Minister doing it, if he has any consideration even for the future welfare of his own party. In 1926 it was said that the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen had not given his followers in the prairies a feather to fly with. I assure the Prime Minister and all members of the cabinet that this is just one of the many millstones that he has hung around the necks of his followers in the west.
Mr. MaoINNIS:	Mr. Chairman, I wish
to say a few words in protest against the resolution. I am amazed, as is the hon. member for Ldsgar, at the Prime Minister in such days as these bringing in the resolution we have before us. I shall be further amazed if his followers support him. If they support him in this measure I cannot understand how they can justify their position in their constituencies when they return home, in view of the position they have taken in regard to other economies which have been made during this and the last sessions.
When we were discussing the ten per cent decrease in civil sendee salaries I drew to the attention of the Minister of Finance the circumstances of a case in my own city where a man with a wife and child was working two and a half hours a day at forty cents an hour. On that dollar a day, which made him

Tariff Board Act
ineligible for relief, he was suffering a ten per cent salary reduction. I asked if situations of that kind could not be obviated, but received no response. Such reductions still go on. I am not opposed to high salaries, but in these days if we are going to increase salaries or wages we should begin by increasing the wages of those who are at the bottom. We should not increase first the salaries of those at the top.
When in 1931 provision was made for a tariff board the salaries of the chairman and the other two members of the board were stated. I presume at that time the Prime Minister felt that $12,000 a year would be sufficient remuneration to obtain the best talent possible. During the last two years the trend of salaries has not been upwards; it has been the reverse. We have been told how the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway have slashed the salaries of their officials. To come at this time and ask for an increase in salary, presumably because the chairman of the tariff board has asked for it, is not fair. If anything would seem to indicate his unfitness for such a high position, it would be that he should come at this time when according to our government the country is in such distress, and (ask for still further remuneration, especially when the salary for which provision had already been made gave him a very fat living, compared with that of the great majority of people in Canada.
A few days ago when the social workers of this dominion were in convention one of the delegates who is in close touch with conditions in the country stated that to-day in Canada 1,600,000 people are on relief. What does that mean? It means that 1,600,000 people, and many more, are on rations, just as if we were under a state of siege. Why should a few people live on the fat of the land while probably fifty per cent of the community are living on rations such as would be handed out in time of famine. Before we begin increasing the salaries of those who are already getting salaries sufficiently high, or too high, I ask that we begin raising the remuneration of those who do not now receive enough to keep body and soul together. Some little time ago I came across an article written by a Canadian woman, the mother of seven children. It appeared in the April issue of Chatelaine, and was so compelling an article that I took pains to find the author, although it had been published anonymously in the magazine. I found the lady in the province of Nova Scotia. I should like to give a few words
from her article by way of indicating the conditions under which she and her family have to live at this time. She says:
I am a Canadian mother.
The most noble calling in the world is mine.
I am a Canadian mother and my country honours me. At banquets I am reverently toasted by Canada's noble sons.
When depression comes, my country rushes to the rescue. But when the S.O.S. goes out, do Canadians cry "Mothers and babies first"?
I am provided with groceries. No milk.
A family of seven children, and provided with no milk!
We are allowed no butter at all, no meat but fat pork for beans. I copy from our bill: II bags flour, 3 pounds shortening, 1 pound tea, 10 pounds sugar, 1 gallon molasses, 10 pounds beans, 4 pounds pork, 6 pounds broken codfish, 10 pounds rolled oats, 2 boxes yeast cakes. This is the allowance for the family of seven for one month.
I would like to bring this woman and her family face to face with a man who is already getting $12,000 a year and ask him if he is justified in requesting another $3,000 a year while this woman with her family has to live under such conditions. I would ask hon. members opposite, how are they going to face their constituents who are on relief and justify to them this increase?
Then we come to the matter of superannuation and retiring allowance. I am in favour of retiring allowances and superannuation for every one, not only a few people who are already getting high wages and are able to take care of themselves. May I ask hon. members opposite, is not the tendency here to work in the opposite direction to need? This is a certain sort of paternalism, which manifests itself in the providing of pensions and retiring allowances for persons receiving high salaries. It would be different if we were asking it for other members of the civil service. Remember that during the last two years the annual increase in salaries and wages of the civil service staff, something that was justly coming to them, has been discontinued, so that they have not only received the ten per cent reduction but in addition have suffered the loss of their annual increase. I protest against the passing of this resolution at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I will only
say a word or two. I could not but notice the contrast between the proceedings yesterday in this house and those of the present sitting. To-day a great part of our time has been taken up with the question of pensions and superannuation for people who least require it. In the motion we are now discussing it is proposed in respect of persons
Tariff Board Act

receiving $10,000 and $15,000 a year that after they have been in the service of the government for ten years they shall be entitled to half their salary as a retiring allowance. In other words the $10,000 a year members of this commission will receive after ten years, if they are over sixty years of age, a retiring allowance of $5,000 a year, and the chairman of the board after he has served ten years and is over sixty will be entitled to a retiring allowance of $7,500 a year.
First of all I object to the increase at this time in the salaries of these highly paid officials. Again I must contrast to-day's proceedings with what took place yesterday when we were discussing the railway bill. During that discussion mention was made of the salaries paid to officials of the Canadian National Railways, and the Minister of Railways took a certain amount of credit for the large reductions made in the salaries of many of those officials, making reference to the fact that in some cases those reductions were as high as forty per cent.
Many of them are still getting higher salaries than this.

Well, I am speaking of the principle, not of particular cases. In this case the government, instead of proceeding consistently with the actions of which they were so proud yesterday, ask us to provide a salary for the chairman of the board twenty-five per cent in excess of what was proposed just a few months ago. When the government practises economy at the expense of even the lowest paid employees, it is a very poor time to ask parliament to grant a twenty-five per cent increase in the salary of a highly paid official of the government service. I remember very well just a few weeks ago when we were discussing civil service salaries it was said that even the charwomen ought to be proud to make some contribution to the state in its hour of difficulty. But here a highly paid officer, who in addition to his salary is promised a very large retiring allowance, instead of being proud to make a contribution in this hour of financial crisis asks a twenty-five per cent increase in the salary originally proposed. What a contrast! As the hon. member for Acadia just says, he does not happen to be a charwoman so he does not have to make the sacrifice.
In connection with pensions or retiring allowances to railway men who perhaps as a result of the legislation passed yesterday will in the very near future find themselves without employment, we were told yesterday by the Minister of Raihvays that he objected to

providing retiring allowances for them because it would be a form of class legislation. Yet lo and behold! within twenty-four hours of that legislation being passed we are asked to provide retiring allowances for judges. I suppose this will be called not class legislation but an act of statesmanship. At this time when salaries are being slashed, when municipalities find it most difficult to provide even the bare necessities of life to the men and women who are unemployed, it will be impossible to justify before our constituents this action on the part of the government.

I wish to make a few observations on this question. Every other hon. member has approached the problem in an attitude of amazement. To-day we have been discussing salaries of judges; we are now discussing the salary of a judge who is to be chairman of this new tariff board. But, Mr. Chairman, I am not amazed. We have seen many leading members of the legal profession doing a good turn for their own fraternity. I am not finding great fault with that. That reflects I suppose a human characteristic in them. But I think the government must agree with this side of the house that when the labour members fought so strenuously to have some provision made for the railway men, there was a great deal of merit in their contention. This government has practised economy with religious zeal. I have always held the opinion that the present state of. agriculture and industry, its make-up, its driving force, is absolutely in opposition to the economy practised by the government of this day. Someone suggested that many applications would have been received if this position had been advertised. I believe there would have been a queue reaching from Ottawa to Vancouver on the one side and from Ottawa to Halifax on the other if that had been done. It is passing strange that when the governments of this country are taking $5 from the pensions of the old people who happen to be living together in the sunset of their lives, they would ask for legislation that has for its purpose an increase of 25 per cent in the salary received by the chairman of a board who already receives $12,000 a year. Let us not forget also that one of the members of this tariff board will be a comparatively young man when he will be entitled to retire on a pension of $5,000 a year.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that in view of the past and anticipated future policy of the government nothing can be said in favour of this measure. I am not so sure-and I am not casting any reflection upon the chairman

Tariff Board Act
of the board-that it would not have been better if some able economist had been appointed to head this tariff board, but that is beside the point. I just want to register my protest with regard to a policy that I consider absolutely wrong in principle, particularly in view of the practice of the government with regard to many other employees in the civil service, and indirectly with regard to the old age pensioners of this country. This granting of increases to people who could well do without them seems to be a studied policy of the government, but I believe we are passing through a time when these high salaries are neither necessary nor sound in the industrial, commercial and governmental life of this dominion.

I do not think there is any need to administer any more of these pin pricks to the Prime Minister; they just seem to put him to sleep. He seems to be saying to himself, "Well, I wish to glory these fellows would quit yapping or do it a little more quietly so I could really sleep." For myself I am really speechless. Ever since the Prime Minister made that outrageous appointment to Washington, which savoured so strongly of the family compact of a hundred y'ears ago, this government has been going from bad to worse in these appointments, and from there to Milton Campbell.
I see the Prime Minister is awake now. If I tried my best to devise a method to turn out communists, bolshevists, reds and all those people whom we do not desire, I could not do better than the government has done. Look at that rearguard bunch of dummies, taking it all; not one of them has approved of it. I will bet that they wish they could rear into it just as I am trying to do. I imagine some of them would give a hundred dollars if they could have ten minutes at their leader. I would not give that much, because I can have it without paying the hundred dollars.
I have no language with which to express my disappointment in the course being pursued by the Prime Minister. We are asked to vote fifteen thousand plunks for a man who has not been on the job long enough to warm the saddle; already he wants an increase of S3,000. I think he should get a hoist from the toe of somebody's boot rather than this sort of hoist in salary. Milton Campbell! Well, I shall not say anything about him; his chief qualification was that he was a political dancing dervish, pretending to be a Progressive when everyone knew he was a hidebound Tory all the time. The people out in the country well know that Milton Campbell has sold himself, and that is the end of the "Progs" out there.
I have been wondering what to say. I obtained a big brown envelope, and into it I slipped a couple of these order papers, and I addressed the envelope to the central Liberal committee in the constituency of Kinistino. I think I will send a few more to the constituency of Mackenzie, just to see what the boys up there think of it. I may have to buy those order papers; to-morrow I may have to put up five cents each for them, but perhaps I will buy a dozen more just so the people in the west may know what has been going on in salary boosting on the hill.
I wonder if the Prime Minister has no shame. To what extent is he going in coughing up these great big salaries to men who are just starting on the job. Milton Campbell! Well, will some person support me? I will need some support soon; I can hardly stand up. That is not all; after these people have been ten years on the job they will get life pensions of $5,000 a year. If for the next ten years the members of this board pursue the policy that, has been fallowed in the past by this government I do not believe they will stay in their positions very long, and there will be no question of pensions involved at all. We hope it will not be too long hence until we get another government, before everything goes to the bow-wows. We heard of some General McNaughton and General MaeBrien or O'Brien or some such name, another of these big mugwumps with the big salaries who was given an increase recently. Out on the farm we have to work bard; my own wife has to work from five o'clock fast time until God knows what time at night. She does not get a look in at this sort of thing and thousands and tens of thousands of other farmers' wives have to work long hours to help to pay these mighty big salaries.
You should be there helping her.

Do you think I
am going to sit here in silence and see the taxes of this country-and like other people we have to put up our share of those taxes- being shovelled into the capacious maws of the friends of the Prime Minister? No, I am not going to keep silent. I was trying-and I thought I had succeeded in doing so-to cultivate a better relationship and a better feeling towards the Prime Minister. No one in this house admires his many abilities more than I do, but it is a pity those wonderful abilities cannot be devoted to better purposes. I would suggest that in future he should not be so almighty generous with other people's money, in regard to salaries. Why was it necessary to increase these salaries; were these
