gentlemen going on strike? I see even the chairman is hiding his face. No wonder; a cloud should come over the land and hide us all for shame. Now I forget what I was saying when the chairman covered his face, so I will have to start all over again. I had some notes here ; I do not know what was on them, but I think this is far more serious than most of us realize at the moment. Fifteen thousand dollars for one year! Why, that looks like a fortune that would last the average farmer a lifetime. I do implore the Prime Minister in justice to himself to stop this kind of extravagance at this time. Wait for two or three years; wait for a few months; even wait until we have turned the comer a bit. We believe we are turning the comer but we shall never get it turned if the Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance are going to be digging into the treasury in this manner. Does this mean that we are going to start all over again, after times have improved a little, and once more enter upon a rampage of borrowing and spending and spreeing? It looks like it and the Prime Minister of Canada is setting the example-he or his Minister of Finance or perhaps-the whole lot of them.
I do not find any pleasure in making these observations, but I am so filled with indignation that for my own safety I have to say these things. I would ask the Prime Minister whether these gentlemen were really going on strike, whether they had refused to work for the salaries they were being paid. I understand that this matter was up yesterday; I did not know it. In fact, I have not yet recovered from the shock I received when I first saw it on the order paper two days ago.
I think I have a right to get an answer to that question I have just asked the Prime Minister, because we all contribute to the taxes of the country more or less, some of us less and some of us more, and we have a right to know why this salary has been raised at -his time so quickly after the appointment of ihese three gentlemen.
I met the three of them. There is nothing wrong with their looks, but we are not paying them for their appearance. I do not know whether they have held a meeting of the tariff board or not. Have they sent in their resignations, may I ask? Who has charge of them anyhow? The Minister of National Revenue perhaps can answer that. Is the board under my good friend? If I get no answer from that quarter I will address my remarks generally. Have they indicated that they cannot continue in the employ of the government unless they are given a considerable more than $12,000 for the chairman and $10,000 apiece for the other two? Someone is saying something.
fMr. Motherwell.]
It may be a very profound observation but I do not catch it. At any rate I am entitled to know why this thing has been done in face of the conditions in the country, on the farm, in the factory and everywhere. How dare this government flout the people with these outrageous salaries at this time?
I have felt pretty hard sometimes towards the people who call themselves communists. What are they? People so inflamed with indignation that they will do anything. I am going to sit down before I begin to feel that way myself.

speechtext:
doing I could have escaped the necessity of coming to this house and asking that this resolution be adopted, and if anyone suggests that it is a pleasurable occupation for a man in my position in life ,to sit here and be attacked in the manner in which I have been to-night by hon. gentlemen opposite, notably by the hon. member who last spoke, he must have a strange idea of what constitutes enjoyment. But it is comprehensible that some person may be willing to render a little public service; that is possible, and when we asked Mr. Justice Sedgewick under those circumstances to accept this position, he said: If I am to accept this position with the insecurity that attaches to it in view of what has been said in the House of Commons, I think I am entitled to the compensation which is mentioned in that resolution, and I agreed; I believe he is if he discharges those duties in a manner worthy of the office which he holds. It is a great responsibility. He is in reality sitting as the arbiter between two governments, between the United Kingdom and Canada. He will hear evidence of expert witnesses from Great Britain and from this dominion. He will hear cases presented on behalf of those who seek to obtain access to our markets under more favourable conditions than now prevail, and the reasons given therefor. He -must examine, analyze and sift testimony for -the purpose of ascertaining to what extent the allegations made support the ends sought. All -these things he must do, and if he is to discharge those duties with the judicial quality that characterizes one who is chairman of a board that commands the respect not -only of Canadians but of those from other countries Who come before this tribunal, then I say that he must be in a position where he is not going to be worried every day whether with to-morrow's sun he will be able to -pay his grocer.
Someone has said that the chairman is on trial. Not only is that true, but there is on trial the whole ability of the Dominion of Canada to appoint at the head of a great board one who will command the respect and confidence not only of his own countrymen but of people from the United Kingdom who come here with their cases under the terms of the conference agreements. That must be considered. If we had appointed some partisan as chairman; if we had selected, as we might have done, someone from the ranks of those who support this party; if we had appointed one who might be described as a party hack, what then? What about the indignation of those who go before that tribunal? What would be thought in the United Kingdom and

other countries of our ability to meet and discharge a great responsibility? When the railways and canals commission in England has to deal with a problem, you will find a great judge at the head of it. When they had the tariff commission, they had Sir Sydney Chapman, Sir George May and another gentleman whose name does not come to my mind at the moment. We have no such reservoir. When we have to go to the bench for the purpose of securing an appointment, we do not do so because they are judges as such, or because I happen to be a member of the legal profession, but because in the very nature of things we must endeavour to secure for the positions the best talent we can command, with the idea in mind that not only will Canadians be proud of the appointment, but that those from other lands who come before that tribunal will say: Here is a man who discharges his duty in a manner worthy of the great traditions that belong to those who sit in judgment upon matters affecting the interests of the country as a whole.
That was the idea in my mind, and actuated and governed entirely by that thought, I sought out Mr. Justice Sedgewick and asked him to accept this position. The terms upon which lie was willing to accept it are those indicated in the resolution and for the reason that may be stated, namely, that he was already discharging a great public service. I may say that the resentment expressed by many members of the legal profession that he should be taken from his position, was widespread. If the committee were interested, I could give the names of members of the profession who said: You must not take this man from us; he is the most brilliant and the best qualified of the judges we have had for years on our bench in the trial division and in connection with bankruptcy. It is not a light or easy thing, may I say to my colleagues in the house, for one to tear up the roots of his home in a community, leave it and come to another city to establish his home. If it is thought the compensation is out of all proportion to the duties that will be performed, I can only say this: Having regard to the rewards that go to members of the legal profession Mr. Justice Sedgewick made a great sacrifice when he went upon the bench, and if my appreciation of the situation is correct, to leave that position and accept this meant sacrifice even although the compensation provided is larger than that which he previously received.
May I make just one or two other observations with respect to the matter? I knew that in time of stress and strain this house might not think this the most desirable thing

Tariff Board Act
to do; yet I say to my colleagues in this House of Commons that canvassing the situation in its entirety and looking over the field in every part of the dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific I know not where I could secure an appointee who would so fully measure up to my conception of the ability required to perform the tasks imposed upon him under the statute as the gentleman who has been selected. I do not believe that the Canadian people in the remote sections of the country will be led astray by the attacks that have been made, the specious appeals to sentiments so easily aroused in days of poverty and hardship, the attempt to raise class against class and man against man. Not since the first day of the record of civilization have all men been of equal capacity or equal ability to discharge obligations and duties and responsibilities, and down through all the ages the remuneration paid to men has sometimes been regarded as entirely out of keeping with the value of the services rendered. I know there are men in this house who think that the late president of the Canadian National Railways, who with all his emoluments of office received ten times this salary, was being paid too much, and yet the Pennsylvania railroad pays a much larger compensation than that 'to one man for the duties he discharges. And so with respect to other lines of railway in the United States, and so with respect to lines of railway in the United Kingdom:. Great executive heads in this country also receive a sum to which $15,000 would in comparison seem a mere pittance.
This position is so much more important than any other that I do not believe you can appeal successfully to the prejudices of people, even in the remotest part of this country by pointing out to them that the government should be condemned because it desires to put in this position the foremost man it can find to reflect credit on the Canadian people in the discharge of great obligations before an international tribunal.
Look at the fees you pay to a lawyer before an international commission, running up sometimes to amounts sufficient to pay the whole cost of this office for ten years. These are mere facts. Look at the auditor general's report and see the fees paid by governments, by this government, with respect to litigation which it did not initiate, fees it was bound to pay. I merely mention these things because I did not intend at any length to traverse the matter beyond saying that as the first minister charged with the responsibility of making this choice. I have no apology to make to my fellow countrymen or to any man for agreeing
to the terms which Mr. Justice Sedgewick suggested if accepting the office meant tearing up the roots of his life in the community in which he lived. I believe that the sober, intelligent common sense of the Canadian people will commend any position taken by [DOT]any prime minister who endeavours to see that the public service is worthily served by worthy public servants.
There has been dragged into this debate to-night a discussion with respect to General McNaughton, who is receiving $2,000 more than he was receiving. General McNaughton is receiving less than his predecessor received and less than his predecessors have received, and I should like to say this, that if we had not done that, we would have lost him. As to the capacity and the quality of General McNaughton. whom I did not know intimately at all until I came to this city as Prime Minister, a great English soldier said to me-not a Canadian soldier-"If this empire were involved in war to-morrow I know of no man I would sooner see at the head of affairs than your McNaughton." That is the conception that others have of a man who is now serving the state, and he is serving the state for a smaller sum than he could receive in at least two other quarters, but he loves the service in which he serves, and he is giving to this country in my judgment in the work that he is at present doing a service that is worthy of the amount that is being paid.
When you talk about the Royal Canadian Mounted Police I shall not to-night pay that tribute to General MacBrien which has been paid to him by those who know his work, from his sovereign down, those who know of his capacity, those who know of his training, those who recall the fact that he served in days long since past as a constable in the police near the city, part of *which I have the honour to represent in this house; those who know his record as a field officer, his record as a general and as an administrator, his record and his capacity to earn a much larger sum than that which we are now paying him. I believe we have saved more money since he took over the duties of that office than he will ever receive in the entire sum that we shall pay to him during the term he serves. I know that his service does not commend itself to everyone. It is not expected it would. His job is to preserve law and order. His job is to put down anarchy. His job is to stamp out lawlessness, and there are many who do not like that.

But I want to go a step further. When the right hon. gentleman appointed a commission, a very proper thing to do, to inquire into the salaries to be paid to what are called the technical officers of this country, it will be recalled that recommendations were made that the salaries should be increased because they were out of all proportion to what might be received if these same men were working for private enterprise and not serving the state. If my memory serves me aright it was pointed out by the right hon. gentleman then leading the government that it was desirable in every way for this dominion to endeavour to secure the services of men who would be sought by private undertakings, and that we should be able to secure just as faithful service to the state as would be rendered by these same men if they served private enterprise. In many instances that has been the case, and I trust that it will continue to be so. I know a great many men serving the state faithfully in these times who by reason of their very qualities could be receiving larger compensation if they served private enterprise where their great talents and abilities would find larger scope and greater opportunities for expression. I mention that because it seems to me I should fairly state what actuated the government in arriving at the conclusion which it reached to accept the suggestion that vTas made, and which I agreed to at once, as to Mr. Justice Sedgewick.

speechtext:
I have in my hands the journals for 1931 and for 1930. Some hon.

members surely will remember that he voted against the government when the motion was made on the first occasion this session for the speaker to leave the chair. And five days before he was appointed he had no idea in the world he was to be approached for that purpose. I think he knows perfectly well he was not the first choice. But because of being unable to secure the gentleman whom we sought to secure, Mr. Campbell, as a western man, was asked to accept the office, and he did. I still believe he is at least not a Conservative, whatever else may be said about him, and that he is not a supporter of this government. His criticisms of this government you will find upon the records of Hansard.
As far as the younger man, the gentleman from Quebec, is concerned, you have there an illustration of what I consider to be the duty of governments with 'respect to the public service. The government could do one of two things. It could select an old and tried supporter, one who, in the language of the right hon. gentleman, was thoroughly imbued with the doctrine of protection, or it could take a young man on the threshold of life, who has been educated in the universities of this country and of Great Britain, who speaks with equal fluency both the official languages of Canada, and who in his father's organization has had practical business experience. We selected a young man with this training, because it is my firm belief that under those circumstances you will get the best service for the state.
That is about all I have to say to the committee as to the factors that influenced us in the appointments that were made. But may I add that the right hon. gentleman made another mistake when he suggested that these commissioners are to receive pensions equal to those paid to judges. It will be remembered that in the statute the salary of the chairman 'is placed at $12,000 and those of the remaining commissioners at $10,000. After serving ten years they might receive one-quarter of their salary as pensions, and after serving at least five years twenty per cent; that is all. As the right hon. gentleman has said, the language of the resolution is general. With respect to the chairman I propose to add after the word "sixty" the word "four" so that it can apply only to the chairman, and to no one else. He is now fifty-five years of age; ten years from the sixth of February last he will be sixty-five. Instead of providing that he should be sixty or over, the resolution will provide that he should attain the age of sixty-four, and the

provision will apply to him and to no one else.
I have spoken longer than I had intended. I repeat that I have neither apologies to make nor regrets to express in regard to this matter. The necessities of cases make it incumbent upon me frequently to make decisions which, quite properly, are subject to criticism. But the position taken in this case is I believe the only one which could properly foe taken having regard to the interests of the state, having regard to the importance of the issues to foe dealt with and the necessity of providing as chairman of this board one who would reflect credit upon Canada both at home and abroad amongst those peoples with whom we have made trade agreements. We must have confidence in his capacity, his integrity, his broad view and his ability to grapple with the problems presented to him.

It is satisfying at least to have been able to awaken the right hon. gentleman from his slumber of a few minutes ago. I do not pretend to be a stickler on ethics in parliament or anywhere else, but when various members had each spoken about a half an hour, while the Prime Minister lolled over as if he did not give a continental who we were or what we were or what we were saying, I thought it was just about time someone gave him a good poke in the eye so as at least to get him up. The right hon. gentleman is an expert at explaining; I admire him from the bottom of my heart. I take my hat off to him. If there is anybody on this earth who can make black appear white and white no colour at all, it is the right hon. gentleman. Now we know just about what his estimate of a proper public man for public .service would be,-that is Milton Campbell, because he says himself he was a Progressive and formerly a Liberal. Saying things does not make them so. Recording. them in that book, whatever it is, does not make them so. Milton Campbell was known to many of us, in the west. I think he did vote for a provincial Liberal once, but that does not make a man a Liberal. I. do not think the Prime Minister would have referred to Hansard if he had. looked it up himself and had seen just what was Mr. Campbell's record since' this government came into power. We also have been looking them up, and we find that he has not voted very often for this side of the house, especially when something could be gained by not doing so. The fact that he drew in what he threw his bait, hook and line after, shows where he stood. To say that he is a Liberal in the face of what has happened is pure nonsense. What are the farmers saying

I do not know where the laugh comes in. Part of the performance was put on by the Prime Minister himself. Why could he not have saved us this humiliation? Could he not have waited a little while before doing this thing? The very fact that these three gentlemen are exacting this money at this time shows that they are not fit for their jobs.
Oh, oh.

Yes, it does. They have not the decency or sensitiveness of a hollow-backed ox or they would not have demanded more money at this time. I say it; I say it again, and I will say it as many times as I like, because it is true. What about the clergymen and school teachers throughout this country, many of them living on miserable, measly salaries paid by people so poverty stricken that they cannot afford to pay more?
No salaries at all.

We want someone on the tariff board who will not be worrying about his grocery bill the Prime Minister says. Fifteen thousand plunks, and worrying about the grocery bills! If some people had one-twentieth of that they would be well satisfied and thought well off. I am sorry that we will have to change our views with regard to the Prime Minister's conception of public duty. Just think of the grab there will be throughout the country if a man knows that all he has to do is to put in a claim that with a salary of $12,000 his grocery bill is worrying, him, and that he wants another $3,000. They will be rushing in from all points of the compass. Why not? I am amazed at the reasoning of the Prime Minister. My right hon. friend is mistaken if he thinks that this country is not shocked at this shovelling out of money when the treasury is so depleted and it is so hard to get it replenished from the taxes. I might as well not try to express my feelings because

I cannot express myself to-night as I would like. It is the way of the evil doer always; if anyone criticizes or objects, the answer is: "Oh, you are making a commotion; they will hear you; someone will be alarmed!" Who is the author of the commotion but the government which pays out these salaries? The government could easily have let a year go by before taking this action; in all conscience that is what should have been done, and then later on when things were getting better they could have done something for them, poor boys! I do not know Judge Sedgewick; he may be a world beater, but as for Milton Campbell-
You used to like him.

The best evidence that this whole house is shocked beyond description is the fact that the hon. member for Marquette is not endeavouring to babble his support of the Prime Minister. They cannot do otherwise if they are to be honest with themselves.

As a former political
neighbour of Milton Campbell, former member for Mackenzie, I think I should correct an impression which may have been created in the minds of the members of the house this evening by the Prime Minister. Mr. Chairman, some time ago I had a definite feeling with respect to appointments to the tariff board, but any feeling I had in favour of the board was absolutely dispelled by the remarks made this evening by the Prime Minister. The tariff board must exist for one of two purposes; it must be a fact finding body to give to the government the information which the government should have in order to decide on the tariff policies of the dominion, or it must be a body sufficiently well equipped to take that duty away from the government and decide on the tariff policies of the country itself. It must be for one of those two purposes. If, as the Prime

Minister said, it is to decide great questions of policy I submit that a worse board could not possibly have been chosen.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Prime Minister did not say that; I hope the hon. gentleman will take it back.

If the Prime Minister did not make that statement I do not need to make any remarks relative thereto, but if the Prime Minister meant that this board was to decide on Canadian tariff policies I say again that a worse board could not have been chosen. To be of any value in deciding the policies of Canada the board should be composed of men having broad political experience, with some knowledge of the needs of the producer and of the consumer. I submit also that a worse board could not have been chosen as a fact finding body. If it is to be a fact finding body the man at the top, the chairman, need not be a judge; there is nothing to decide. Of course hearings must be held, but the man at the head of the board should be the most eminent economist in the Dominion, a man who can use our national statistics; compile figures from the evidence which will be heard, and submit to the government conclusive calculations showing exactly what will be the economic effect upon the general industrial fabric of this dominion of any specific tariff action. Judge Sedgewick is a gentleman for whom I have a very high regard. I do not object at all to the salaries of the members of the tariff board being substantial amounts; I am not now dealing with that point. However, certainly Judge Sedgewick's training has not been along the line of economics; his training has been in interpreting the statutes which are passed or amended by parliament from year to year. The duty of a judge is to determine whether or not a man is guilty of an offence under the laws of the country. The training of a judge is far different from that of a man who is required to compile statistics to submit conclusions to the government by whom the final judgment must be made.
Then, Mr. Chairman, if it is to be a fact finding body it does seem to me that industry in Canada has a perfect right to have someone on the board who knows the industrial condition of the country and who will be in a position intelligently to question British manufacturers when they come here to make their submissions as to why their products should be admitted to Canada at lower rates of duty. I think also that on the board there should be someone representing the purchasing public of Canada, whether it be from the standpoint of the importers or of the consumers.
